title: Why Some Data Stories Stick and Others Don’t
subtitle: The four simple elements behind every memorable data story
body_html:
Most data stories are kind of forgettable.

They have nice charts.

They show the right numbers.

But five minutes later, no one remembers what it was about.

That’s the tough part about data storytelling.

It’s not that they’re wrong.

Or boring.

They just don’t stick.

It’s not just about being right. It’s about being remembered.

Here are 4 things great data stories almost always have:

1. A little surprise

If everything in your story is expected, no one pays attention.

We remember what surprises us.

Even small things.

A number that doesn’t fit.

A result that flips a common belief.

A pattern no one saw coming.

Find that moment.

Make it the hook.

Let the data pull people in.

2. Clean, clear visuals

If someone has to squint or think too hard to read your chart… it’s over.

You don’t need to show everything.

You need to show the point.

Use one main chart.

Keep the text light.

Highlight the key number.

Make it obvious.

When the visual is clear, the message comes through faster.

3. A human angle

Data hits harder when people see themselves in it.

So go beyond the metric.

Show what it means for real people.

Fewer clicks on the website? Maybe that’s fewer signups.

Fewer signups? Maybe that’s a missed opportunity for someone looking for help.

Numbers are just the starting point.

Add a little heart, and people care more.

4. One big takeaway

The best stories don’t try to say five things at once.

They say one thing well.

So don’t make your audience guess what matters.

Tell them.

“This is the trend.”

“This is the risk.”

“This is the opportunity.”

Make your message so clear they could sum it up in a sentence, without needing your slides.

Here’s the bottom line:

If you want your work to be remembered, don’t just present.

Tell a story.

Make it clear.

Make it human.

Make it stick.

And don’t wait for it to be perfect.

Practice with the project you’re working on right now.

Your next insight might be the one that actually gets people to listen.

If this helped, there’s more where that came from. Subscribe to get the next one. It’s free.

title: What Hollywood Can Teach Us About Dashboards
subtitle: Dashboards Deserve a Good Script Too
body_html:
When you think of dashboards, Hollywood probably isn’t the first thing that comes to mind.
But they actually have a lot in common.

Movies and dashboards both tell stories.
They both need to grab attention.
And the best ones leave people with a clear, satisfying “aha” at the end.

So what can dashboard builders learn from filmmakers?

1. Set the Scene

Make It Easy to Follow from the Start

Every good movie starts by setting things up.
We learn where we are, who’s involved, and what matters.

Dashboards should do the same.
If people have to guess what they’re looking at, you’ve already lost them.

Dashboard Tip:
Use the top section to show the big picture.
Highlight key metrics, add simple titles, and make sure the layout is clean and clear.

Think about the opening of The Lion King. We meet Simba, see the world around him, and get a feel for what’s coming.

2. Build Tension

Let the Story Unfold Naturally

A good movie builds interest as it goes.
The challenge gets bigger. Questions start to form. People get invested.

Your dashboard should do that too.
Each section should build on the last and guide your viewer toward a key insight.

Dashboard Tip:
Use charts that show movement, change, or contrast.
Help people spot problems, trends, or surprises.

Think about Avengers: Infinity War. Every time Thanos finds a stone, the pressure builds.

3. Stick the Landing

Leave Your Viewer with Something Clear

By the end of a story, we want answers.
We want to know what happened, why it matters, and what comes next.

Your dashboard should make that easy.

Dashboard Tip:
End with a clear “So what?”
Help people walk away knowing what matters most.

Think about the end of Finding Nemo. Marlin changes, the story wraps up, and we walk away with a clear message.

You don’t need to be a filmmaker to build a great dashboard.
You just need to think like a storyteller.

Start with the big picture.
Guide people through the details.
End with something they can act on.

Because when data tells a good story, people pay attention.

title: SteaI the layout before you build the dashboard
subtitle: Because designing from scratch is overrated.
body_html:
Here's a secret that pro designers have been using forever: they don't start from scratch. They "borrow" ideas, mix them up, and create something new. And you can totally do the same thing with your dashboards.

Most of us jump straight into our BI tool and start throwing charts around like we're decorating a room blindfolded. We end up with dashboards that look like a data explosion happened. Numbers everywhere. Confusing layouts, and colors that make your eyes hurt.

But great dashboards aren't born from pure creativity. They're born from smart inspiration.

The Designer's Playbook (That Works for Data Too)

Graphic designers, web designers, and UX folks have a process that's been working for decades:

  1. Look at what's already working

  2. Take notes on the good stuff

  3. Sketch their own version

  4. Build it out

Sounds simple, right? That's because it is.

Step 1: Become a Dashboard Detective

Start hunting for dashboard inspiration in these goldmine spots:

Tableau Public: This is like the Instagram of dashboards. Search for anything – sales dashboards, HR analytics, marketing reports. You'll find thousands of examples from real analysts just like you.

Dribbble and Behance: These are where designers show off their best work. Search "dashboard UI" or "analytics dashboard" and prepare to have your mind blown by the clean, beautiful layouts.

Pinterest: Don't laugh. Pinterest has some seriously good dashboard inspiration boards. Search "data dashboard design" or "business intelligence layout."

Pro tip: Don't just look at dashboards in your industry. A marketing dashboard might have the perfect layout for your sales report, and a finance dashboard could inspire your HR analytics.

Step 2: Screenshot Like Your Job Depends on It

When you find layouts you like, don't just think "that's nice" and move on. Take screenshots and really study them:

  • Where do they put the big important numbers? (Usually at the top where your eye goes first)

  • How do they group related charts together? (Notice the invisible boxes that organize everything)

  • What colors do they use? (Spoiler: usually fewer than you think)

  • How much white space is there? (More than you'd expect. It's not wasted space, it's breathing room)

Create a folder on your computer called "Dashboard Inspiration" and start collecting. Trust me, future you will thank present you.

Step 3: Sketch Before You Click

This step separates the pros from the amateurs, and it takes maybe 10 minutes.

Grab whatever's handy – a notebook, the back of an envelope, PowerPoint, even a napkin. Draw boxes where things should go:

  • Big box at the top for your key metrics (your KPIs that everyone cares about most)

  • Medium boxes for your main charts

  • Small boxes for filters and controls

  • Don't forget space between everything

Think of it like planning where furniture goes in a room before you start moving heavy stuff around.

Here's what to consider while sketching:

  • What's the most important thing? Put it where people look first (top left, then top center)

  • What goes together? Group related charts near each other

  • How will people use this? Put filters where they're easy to find but not in the way

Step 4: Build with Your Blueprint

Now open up your BI tool and use your sketch as a rough guide. Don't stress about making it pixel-perfect. Your sketch is just the starting point.

As you build, you'll naturally make adjustments. Maybe that chart needs to be bigger than you thought, or the colors need tweaking, or the filters might work better on the left instead of the right.

That's totally normal. Your sketch got you 80% of the way there, and now you're fine-tuning the last 20%.

Why This Actually Works

Your brain is wired to recognize patterns. When you see a layout that "feels right," it's because it follows design principles that humans naturally respond to. Things like visual hierarchy, balance, and grouping.

By starting with layouts that already work, you're building on top of proven design psychology instead of trying to reinvent it from scratch.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Don't copy everything exactly – You're not trying to create a duplicate. You're borrowing the structure and making it work for your data.

Don't skip the sketching – I know it feels like an extra step, but it saves you hours of moving things around later.

Don't overthink the colors – Most great dashboards use 2-3 colors max. Pick one main color, one accent color, and stick with grays for everything else.

Don't cram everything in – If your dashboard needs a scroll bar, it's probably trying to do too much. Sometimes the best design decision is to split things into multiple dashboards.

You're Not Cheating

Some people feel weird about "stealing" design ideas. But here's the reality: every designer, artist, and creator builds on what came before them. There's a reason certain dashboard layouts show up everywhere. They work.

You're not copying someone's data or analysis. You're learning from their smart layout decisions and applying those lessons to your own work.

Your Action Plan

  1. This week: Spend 30 minutes browsing Tableau Public or Dribbble for dashboard inspiration

  2. Save 5-10 screenshots of layouts you like

  3. Pick your next dashboard project (even a small one)

  4. Sketch it out first using one of your inspiration layouts as a starting point

  5. Build and see the difference

Great dashboards don't start from scratch. They start from inspiration.

So don't reinvent the layout. Steal it smart, make it yours, and watch your dashboards go from "meh" to "wow, who made this?"

Your data deserves a layout that makes it shine. And now you know exactly how to give it one.

title: What Does 7.3 Even Mean? Why Context Matters
subtitle: Why Most Dashboards Confuse People (and How to Fix It)
body_html:
If I told you I ran a mile in 8 minutes, you might think, “Cool, good for you.”

But if I told you I’m 65 years old and just started running six months ago, suddenly that 8-minute mile becomes pretty impressive.

Same number, completely different story.

This is exactly what happens in the data world every single day.

We get so excited about our findings that we forget the most important part. Helping people understand what those numbers actually mean.

Picture a meeting where someone proudly announces, “Our customer satisfaction score is 7.3.”

Everyone nods politely. Some people even smile.

But here’s the thing. Nobody in that room actually knows if 7.3 is worth celebrating or if it’s time to hit the panic button.

Why Context Makes or Breaks Your Data Story

Data works the same way.

A number without context is just math homework that nobody wants to do. Your audience needs to know if 23 percent is amazing or terrible before they will care about your analysis.

The problem is that we analysts live and breathe our data every day.

We know that 7.3 customer satisfaction is actually pretty bad because we have seen the historical trends and industry benchmarks.

But our audience does not have that context in their brain. They are hearing that number for the first time.

How to Add Context That Actually Helps

Here is the good news. Adding context does not require fancy tools or complicated analysis.

You just need to answer three simple questions every time you share a number.

1. Compared to what?
Always give your audience a reference point.

Compare your number to last month, last year, or the industry average.

Saying “Our conversion rate dropped to 2.1 percent, which is down from 2.8 percent last quarter” tells a very different story than just “Our conversion rate is 2.1 percent.”

2. What does good look like?
Set clear expectations about what success means.

If you are tracking website bounce rate, do not just say it is 45 percent.

Tell them that anything under 40 percent is considered excellent in your industry.
That 40 to 55 percent is average.
And anything above 55 percent needs attention.

3. Why should they care?
Connect your number to something that matters to your audience.

Instead of saying “Email open rates are 18 percent,”
try “Email open rates are 18 percent, which means we are reaching about 1,800 fewer customers than we could be with industry-standard performance.”

Real Examples That Show the Difference

Let’s see how context changes everything.

Without context: “Sales increased 15 percent this month.”
With context: “Sales increased 15 percent this month. That beats our 10 percent target and is our best performance since the holiday season.”

Without context: “Website traffic is down 8 percent.”
With context: “Website traffic dropped 8 percent last week. But that is actually normal for this time of year. We saw the same seasonal dip in 2023 and 2022.”

Without context: “Customer support tickets increased to 47 per day.”
With context: “Customer support tickets jumped to 47 per day. That is double our usual volume and explains why response times have been slower.”

See how much more useful those become?

The numbers are the same. But now your audience actually knows what to do with the information.

Making Context a Habit

The best part about adding context is that it becomes automatic once you start doing it.

Every time you are about to share a number, just pause and ask yourself:

“If I heard this number for the first time, would I know if it is good or bad?”

If the answer is no, add the context.

Your audience will thank you.
Your recommendations will be clearer.
Your data stories will lead to action instead of confusion.

Start with your next presentation or report.

Pick one key metric and make sure you explain not just what it is, but what it means.

You will be surprised how much more engaged your audience becomes when they actually understand the story your data is telling.

Remember this. A number without context is just a number.

A number with context is insight that can change how people think and act.

That is the difference between being a data reporter and being a data storyteller.

title: Stop Being the Dashboard Color Police
subtitle: Why Conditional Formatting Is Your Secret Weapon
body_html:
Let’s do some quick math that might make you uncomfortable.

If you spend just 30 minutes each week manually updating dashboard colors and status indicators…
That adds up to 26 hours per year.

At the average analyst salary, that’s $1,300+ spent on something a computer should be doing for free.

But the real cost isn’t just time. It’s the mistakes.

Remember that one week you forgot to change a key metric from green to red?
Your stakeholders made decisions based on the wrong signal.
By the time anyone noticed, the issue had already grown worse.

Manual updates also lead to inconsistency.
Your “bad” might be someone else’s “almost okay,”
and soon your dashboard speaks five different visual languages.

Let’s fix that.

What Is Conditional Formatting?

Conditional formatting is like giving your dashboard a brain.

It’s a simple set of rules that change the look of your data based on the values inside.
If a number drops below target, it turns red.
If it hits a new high, it glows green, all on its own.

Think of it as a traffic light system for your metrics.
You set the rules once, and your visuals update automatically as the data changes.

It’s not just about making things colorful.
It’s about creating visual cues your brain can understand instantly before you even read the number.

Real-Life Ways to Use It

Here are four practical formatting systems that work in real dashboards:

1. The Traffic Light System

Use red, yellow, and green to show performance at a glance.
Go further by using gradients; light green for “barely made it,” dark green for “crushing it.”

2. The Heat Map

Great for comparing lots of values across products, time periods, or regions.
Let your eyes do the scanning. The hottest or coldest spots pop out instantly.

3. The Progress Bar

Show completion or goal tracking with bars that fill and change color.
It’s like turning your metrics into a video game, and yes, it’s way more engaging.

4. The Anomaly Detector

Use formatting to flag things that stand out, like sudden spikes or drops.
You’ll spot problems before they become full-blown issues.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Even conditional formatting can go wrong if you’re not careful. Watch out for these:

❌ Too Many Colors

A rainbow dashboard looks fun but tells no story. Stick to 3–4 consistent colors max.

❌ Only Red and Green

Real data has nuance. Add yellow or use gradients to show shades of performance.

❌ Changing Color Rules Too Often

If your red this month means what yellow meant last month, no one will trust the dashboard.
Consistency is key.

❌ Arbitrary Thresholds

Make sure your rules reflect business reality.
If 85% is a win for your team, don’t make it look like a fail just because it’s under 90%.

The Future: Smarter Dashboards

Conditional formatting is just the beginning.

Some dashboards already use machine learning to update visuals based on trends, seasonality, or even weather.

Soon, we’ll move from dashboards that react...
to dashboards that predict.

Colors that adapt to context.
Formatting that spots patterns you didn’t even think to look for.

And it all starts with simple rules.

Your Next Move

Don’t try to fix everything at once.

Start with one key metric.
Add a traffic light rule; red, yellow, green.
Let it run for a week. See what changes.

Then slowly add more rules, gradients, and connected logic.
Make formatting part of your data story.

You’ll spend less time fixing visuals
and more time finding insight.

Because the goal isn’t to eliminate your role.
It’s to stop wasting brainpower on things a dashboard can do.
So you can focus on what really matters.

title: The Only 5 Charts You’ll Ever Need (According to Google Trends)
subtitle: If you’re new to data viz, start with these
body_html:
When it comes to data visualization, most people do not need fancy or complex charts. In fact, Google Trends shows that just five chart types dominate the internet.

And chances are, these are the only ones you will ever need to tell a clear and powerful story with your data.

Let’s go through them one by one, including how and when to use each one effectively.

Just so you know: All data visualizations in this article use synthetic or illustrative data for learning purposes only.

1. Bar Chart

Use it for: Comparing categories, ranking items, or showing parts of a whole

Bar charts are the most searched and most used chart type in the world. And for good reason. They are simple, flexible, and easy to read.

There are three main types:

i) Vertical Bar Chart (Column Chart)
This is best for comparing things like product sales or app downloads.
Example: TikTok was actually the most downloaded app in 2020, not Zoom, even though Zoom got more attention. The bar chart made that easy to see.

ii) Horizontal Bar Chart
This works better when you have more categories, ideally between seven and fifteen.
Example: It can show who received the most Oscar nominations or how candidates performed in an election.

iii) Stacked Bar Chart
This version helps you break each bar into segments.
Example: Instead of just showing total downloads, you can split each bar into downloads from the USA versus the rest of the world. Just be careful not to add too many segments, or the chart becomes confusing.

💡 Quick tip:
Use vertical bars if you have fewer than seven categories. Switch to horizontal bars when you have more.

2. Histogram

Use it for: Showing how data is distributed across a range

Histograms may look like bar charts, but they serve a different purpose. Instead of comparing categories, they show how values are spread out across a continuous variable like age, income, or time.

Example: A histogram of US household income helps you see how many people fall into different income brackets.

Another great use is the population pyramid. One glance shows you the age structure of a country. The US pyramid highlights an aging population. The Nigerian version shows a much younger one.

3. Pie Chart

Use it with caution: Only use it for very simple part-to-whole comparisons

Pie charts are widely used, but many data experts avoid them. The human brain finds it hard to compare angles and areas, especially when there are many slices.

If you really want to use a pie chart, follow these rules:

  • Keep it to five slices or fewer

  • Start with the largest slice at the top right (like the 12 o'clock position on a clock)

  • Label slices directly so people do not need to check a legend

  • Use color to highlight the most important slice

Example: A pie chart with dozens of small slices makes it almost impossible to spot the third most downloaded app. A bar chart shows it immediately.

4. Scatter Plot

Use it for: Showing relationships between two variables

Scatter plots are powerful tools. They help you discover:

  • Positive or negative trends

  • Whether there is no relationship at all

  • Clusters of similar points

  • Outliers that do not follow the pattern

These charts are great for questions like:
Does screen time affect test scores?
Or do taller people earn more?

5. Line Chart

Use it for: Showing change over time

Line charts are perfect for tracking anything that changes over time, such as stock prices, temperatures, website visits, or monthly revenue.

A great example is a line chart showing how search interest in "line chart" changed throughout 2024. Interest stays fairly steady, with a slight dip around July and a noticeable rise in the fall, peaking in October, possibly during report season.

So you do not need to learn every chart out there to communicate data well. Focus on mastering these five:

  • Bar Chart for comparisons and rankings

  • Histogram for understanding distributions

  • Pie Chart for simple part-to-whole views

  • Scatter Plot for relationships and trends

  • Line Chart for tracking changes over time

Instead of chasing complicated charts, focus on telling a clear story.

title: The NASA Dashboard Effect
subtitle: Signs you’ve gone too far with filters, and how to fix it
body_html:
What's worse than a dashboard with no filters? A dashboard with ALL the filters.

The ones where you need to make 47 decisions before you can see a single chart.

If your users are spending more time setting up filters than actually analyzing data, you might be dealing with what I call "The Filter Frenzy."

This is one of the most common dashboard mistakes that even experienced analysts make. Trust me, we've all been there. We think more options equals more value, but sometimes less really is more.

The Problem: Too Many Choices Paralyze Users

Having too many options makes people do less, not more.

When users see 20 different ways to slice data, they freeze up. They spend 10 minutes trying to figure out which filter to use first.

Users want answers fast, and if they have to click through five dropdowns just to see basic sales numbers, they'll probably just ask someone else instead.

The Solution: The KISS Method

KISS stands for "Keep It Simple, Smarty" (okay, maybe the last word is different, but you get the idea).

Rule 1: The Magic Question

Before adding any filter, ask yourself: "Will users actually need this 80% of the time?" If no, don't add it. That filter for "Left-handed employees born on Tuesdays" seems clever, but nobody's using it.

Rule 2: Start with the Big Three

Most dashboards only need three types of filters:

  1. Time (last month, last quarter, last year)

  2. Location (region, country, store)

  3. Category (product type, department, customer segment)

Three filters can handle 90% of what people need to know.

Rule 3: The 5-Filter Limit

Never put more than 5 filters on a single dashboard page. Five is the magic number because people can remember 5 things easily, they fit nicely on screens, and you can't create analysis paralysis with just 5 options.

Rule 4: Smart Defaults

Set default values for your filters. If 80% of users want "Last 30 Days" data, make that the default. Think of it like Netflix recommendations, Most people just want something good without thinking too hard.

Advanced Tricks When You Need More Complexity

Progressive Disclosure: Start simple, then reveal complexity. Show 3 main filters upfront, then have an "Advanced Filters" button for power users.

Contextual Filtering: Only show filters that make sense. If they're viewing sales data, don't show HR filters.

Search Instead of Dropdowns: Let people type "California" instead of scrolling through 50 states.

Quick Pro Tips

  • Watch real users – Sit behind someone using your dashboard. You'll learn more in 10 minutes than in 10 meetings.

  • Track filter usage – If nobody clicks a filter after 3 months, delete it.

  • Name things clearly – Call it "Date Range," not "Temporal Range Selector."

Your job isn't to show off how many ways you can slice data. It's to help people get answers quickly so they can make better decisions.

Remember: The best dashboard is the one people actually use. And people use simple things that work, not complex things that impress.

title: Eight Questions Every Dashboard Must Answer
subtitle: (And Why Most Dashboards Fail at Half of Them)
body_html:
Every useful dashboard needs to answer eight simple questions. I keep these written on a sticky note next to my monitor because they're that important:

  1. What happened?

  2. When?

  3. Where?

  4. How much?

  5. Compared to what?

  6. Why?

  7. Who cares?

  8. What next?

These aren't just nice-to-have features. They're the foundation of every decision your dashboard needs to support.

Miss one, and you've got a pretty picture that doesn't drive action.

Let's dig into each question and see why they matter.

Question 1: What Happened?

This seems obvious, right? Your dashboard shows sales numbers, website visits, or customer complaints. But here's where most people get it wrong.

"Sales were $50,000" isn't answering "what happened." That's just a number floating in space.

"Sales hit $50,000, our second-best month this year" tells a story. Now we know something actually happened worth paying attention to.

Write chart titles that include the actual event or change, not just the metric name.

Question 2: When?

Time context makes everything meaningful. But you'd be amazed how many dashboards show numbers without clear time references.

I once saw a dashboard that showed "Customer Satisfaction: 4.2/5." Sounds good, right? But when was this measured? Last week? Last year? During the busy season or slow season?

Time isn't just about dates. It's about understanding whether this information is still relevant for the decisions you need to make today.

Always include time ranges prominently. Make it crystal clear when your data is from and how current it is.

Question 3: Where?

Geography matters, but "where" goes beyond maps. It could mean:

  • Which department

  • Which product line

  • Which customer segment

  • Which marketing channel

  • Which store location

The point is helping people understand the scope of what they're looking at. Are we talking about the entire company or just the west coast? All customers or just the premium ones?

Be specific about scope in your titles and labels. "West Coast Sales" is better than just "Sales." "Premium Customer Churn" is clearer than "Customer Churn."

Question 4: How Much?

This is the one question most dashboards actually answer well. Numbers everywhere! Charts galore!

But here's the thing: raw numbers without context are just trivia. "We had 1,247 website visitors" doesn't mean much by itself.

The real question is whether 1,247 is good, bad, or completely normal. Which brings us to...

Question 5: Compared to What?

This is where most dashboards start falling apart. They show you current numbers but forget to give you anything to compare them to.

Comparison is what turns data into insight. Here are the comparisons that actually matter:

  • Compared to last month/quarter/year: Shows trends

  • Compared to our goal: Shows performance

  • Compared to last year same time: Accounts for seasonality

  • Compared to industry average: Shows competitive position

Without comparison, you're just looking at numbers in isolation. With comparison, you can actually judge whether those numbers are good or bad.

Every important metric needs at least one comparison point. If your dashboard shows current sales, also show last month's sales. If it shows customer satisfaction, include your target score.

Question 6: Why?

Here's where things get interesting. And where most dashboards completely give up.

Your dashboard shows that sales dropped 15% last month. Great. But why did that happen? Was it seasonal? Did a competitor launch something new? Did we change our pricing?

Most dashboard builders think "why" isn't their job. They're wrong. You don't need to solve every mystery, but you should help people start asking the right questions.

Use annotations to highlight unusual patterns. Add context boxes that explain known factors. Include links to deeper analysis. Give people a starting point for investigation.

Question 7: Who Cares?

This might sound harsh, but it's crucial. Not every piece of data matters to every person. A good dashboard helps people figure out what they should pay attention to.

Your CEO doesn't need to see individual customer complaint details.

Your customer service manager doesn't need to see quarterly investor metrics.

But somehow, we keep building dashboards that show everything to everyone.

Design different views for different roles. Use alert systems to highlight what needs attention. Make it easy for people to find their most important metrics quickly.

Question 8: What Next?

This is the big one. The question that separates useful dashboards from pretty wall decorations.

After someone looks at your dashboard, what should they do? If the answer is "nothing" or "I don't know," then you've built a reporting tool, not a decision-making tool.

Great dashboards point toward action. They don't just show problems; they suggest solutions. They don't just display metrics; they highlight opportunities.

Include recommended actions for different scenarios. Add links to relevant tools or processes. Design alerts that connect to workflows. Make the path from insight to action as short as possible.

Building Better Dashboards

The good news? Once you know what questions to ask, building better dashboards becomes much easier.

Start every dashboard project by writing down these eight questions. For each chart you plan to include, make sure you can answer at least five of them. If you can't, either redesign the chart or reconsider whether you need it.

The goal isn't to cram all eight answers into every single chart. The goal is to make sure your dashboard as a whole addresses all eight questions for the decisions it needs to support.

Which of these eight questions does your team skip most often? Take a look at your current dashboards and see where the gaps are.

The answers might surprise you. And fixing those gaps might be the difference between dashboards that get used and dashboards that get ignored.

Because at the end of the day, the best dashboard isn't the prettiest one. It's the one that helps people make better decisions faster. And that only happens when you answer all eight questions that matter.

title: The Beginner’s Guide to Cleaner Data Visuals
subtitle: Six ways to make your charts easier on the eyes (and brain)
body_html:
Not every chart needs to be perfect. But every chart should be easy to read.

That doesn't mean using bold colors or flashy designs. It means making smart, simple choices that help your message land. Small things, like font size or spacing, can do a lot of heavy lifting.

And you don't need to be a designer to get it right.

These six tweaks are simple, practical, and tested. Try them out, and see how your charts feel less noisy and more helpful.

1. Make Your Font Bigger

This one's so simple it hurts. Yet we still squint at tiny text all the time.

Nobody likes playing detective just to read your axis labels. When you bump up your font size, people can actually focus on your insights instead of straining to see what you wrote.

If you think your font is big enough, make it bigger. Start with 12pt minimum for any text in your charts, and go even bigger for titles and headers. Your audience will thank you.

2. Add Some Breathing Room (Whitespace)

Cramming everything together is like shouting in someone's face. Give your elements space to breathe.

Our brains process information better when it's not all smooshed together. Add padding around your charts, between sections, and around text blocks. Think of whitespace as your friend, not wasted space.

It guides the eye and reduces overwhelm. Double the space you currently have around your chart elements and see how much calmer everything feels.

3. Left-Align Your Labels

Center-aligned text might look fancy, but it's harder to scan quickly.

When everything starts from the same point, your brain doesn't have to work as hard to find where each line begins.

Left-align your labels, legends, and text blocks to create a clean edge that your eye can follow. Check your current charts and see if your labels are all over the place. Line them up on the left and watch how much easier they become to read.

4. Soften Those Grid Lines

Bold, dark grid lines are like that person who talks too loud in meetings. They take over everything.

Grid lines should help, not distract. Make them light gray or remove them completely. Soft grid lines give context without competing with your data, letting your actual data points become the stars of the show.

Change your grid lines to 20% opacity gray, or try removing them entirely and see if you even miss them.

5. Write Clear Headers That Actually Help

"Chart 1" is not a header. It's a missed opportunity.

Good headers are like road signs for your insights. They tell people exactly what they're looking at and help them understand your data faster. Be specific and helpful.

Instead of “Dashboard” or “Overview,” try "Monthly Sales by Region” or “Website Traffic by Source." See how much more useful that is?

Your headers should set expectations and guide people to your main point.

6. Stick to One Accent Color

Rainbow charts might seem fun, but they're usually just confusing.

One accent color draws attention to what matters most. Too many colors make everything compete for attention, and nothing stands out.

Pick one color for highlighting important data and use gray for everything else. Take your most colorful chart and make everything gray except the most important data point. Notice how your eye goes straight to what actually matters?

The Magic Is in the Combo

Each tweak is small on its own. But when you combine them, things start to click.

Don’t feel like you have to fix everything all at once. That’s a fast track to burnout.

Pick just ONE tweak from this list and apply it to something you’re working on today. See how it feels.

Then come back and share what you tried. What changed? What did you notice?

title: Excel Isn’t Going Anywhere
subtitle: Why Excel Still Rules the Business World (And Always Will)
body_html:
Data professionals love to hate Excel.

We roll our eyes when stakeholders ask for CSV exports.

We cringe when someone mentions pivot tables in planning meetings.

We dream of a world where everyone uses proper databases and modern analytics tools.

But here's the uncomfortable truth: Excel isn't going anywhere. In fact, it's getting stronger.

While we've been busy learning Python and building dashboards, Excel quietly became even more powerful. It added AI features, cloud collaboration, and better data connections.

It evolved while staying exactly what it always was: the tool that everyone actually uses.

Let me explain why Excel still dominates business decisions, and why fighting this reality makes us less effective as data professionals.

Everyone Already Knows How to Use It

Walk into any office building. Ask ten random people to open Excel and create a basic chart. Nine of them can do it without help.

Now ask those same people to write a SQL query. Or create a Python visualization. Or build something in Tableau.

You'll get blank stares.

This isn't about intelligence. It's about accessibility. Excel has been the universal business language for over 30 years. People learned it in school, at their first job, from their colleagues. It's passed down like cultural knowledge.

The network effect is massive.

When everyone knows the same tool, collaboration becomes effortless.

No training required. No special software to install. No IT approval process. Just open the file and start working.

That's the accessibility gap in action.

No Barriers to Entry

Modern analytics tools are powerful. They're also complicated.

Want to use Tableau? That's $70 per user per month.

Need Python for analysis? Time to learn programming.

Prefer R for statistics? Hope you like debugging error messages.

Building dashboards in Power BI? Get ready for licensing discussions with IT.

Excel comes with Microsoft Office. Most businesses already have it. Everyone's computer can run it. There's no procurement process, no user limits, no server requirements.

Friction kills adoption.

Every extra step between someone and their analysis reduces the chance they'll actually do the analysis.

Excel removes friction. It's right there, ready to use, whenever inspiration strikes.

Perfect for Real Business Problems

Most business analysis isn't rocket science. It's:

  • Comparing this month to last month

  • Adding up budget numbers

  • Creating simple charts for presentations

  • Organizing lists of customers or products

  • Calculating basic percentages and totals

Excel handles all of this beautifully.

More importantly, it handles the messy reality of business data. The weird formatting. The mixed data types. The random notes in cells. The "temporary" calculations that become permanent.

Complex tools are overkill for simple problems.

Building a database for a one-time analysis is like using a forklift to move a coffee cup. It works, but it's ridiculous.

Modern analytics tools want clean, structured data. Business reality is messy, unstructured data.

Excel bridges that gap without complaint.

Instant Sharing and Collaboration

Send someone an Excel file. They can open it immediately, make changes, and send it back. No login required. No software to download. No compatibility issues.

Try doing that with a Jupyter notebook. Or a Tableau workbook. Or a Power BI report.

Email is still the dominant collaboration platform in business.

And Excel files travel through email perfectly. They open on any computer. They display the same way for everyone. They print properly for meetings.

Yes, there are better collaboration tools. But "better" doesn't matter if people don't use them.

Excel collaboration works because it fits into existing workflows seamlessly.

Visual Flexibility

Excel charts look exactly how business people expect charts to look. Clean, professional, familiar.

They paste into PowerPoint presentations without issues.

They print clearly on paper.

They follow standard business formatting conventions.

Modern visualization tools can create stunning, interactive charts. But stunning isn't always what you need. Sometimes you just need a simple bar chart that looks professional in a board presentation.

Excel charts speak the visual language of business.

They use colors and formatting that feel appropriate in corporate settings. They don't require explanation or training to interpret.

Plus, making quick changes is effortless.

Need to adjust colors? Double-click and pick new ones.

Want to change the title? Click and type.

Need to add more data? Just expand the range.

Compare that to rebuilding visualizations in other tools every time stakeholders want small changes.

Handles Uncertainty and Experimentation

Business analysis is full of "what if" questions.

What if sales grow by 10% instead of 5%?

What if costs increase more than expected?

What if we launch that new product six months early?

Excel is perfect for this kind of exploratory thinking. Change a number, see what happens. Try different scenarios quickly. Build simple models that anyone can understand and modify.

Excel encourages experimentation.

People aren't afraid to play with numbers because they know they can always undo changes. This leads to better business understanding through hands-on exploration.

Advanced tools often require rebuilding analysis for each scenario.

Excel lets you test ideas in real-time during meetings. That immediacy creates better discussions and faster decisions.

The Bottom Line

Excel dominates business because it solves real problems for real people.

It's accessible, flexible, and familiar. It handles the messiness of business data without requiring technical expertise.

Modern analytics tools are powerful and important. But they complement Excel, they don't replace it.

The most effective data professionals understand this.

They use the right tool for each situation.

Sometimes that's Python for complex analysis. Sometimes it's Tableau for interactive dashboards. And sometimes it's good old Excel for simple, clear communication.

The best tool isn't always the most advanced tool. It's the tool that gets the job done for the people who need to use it.

What's your relationship with Excel these days? Are you embracing it as part of your toolkit, or still trying to convince everyone to use something else?

title: The Chart Building Process That Changed How I Present Data
subtitle: How to think like a storyteller when building your next chart
body_html:
Most charts fail because we skip the thinking part and jump straight to the clicking part.

We open Excel or Tableau, dump in our data, pick the first chart type that looks decent, and call it done.

But your chart is trying to communicate something important. If you don't know what that something is, how can you expect your audience to figure it out?

That's where this process comes in. It forces you to think before you build. And trust me, your future self will thank you for it.

Step 1: Analyze Requirements & Choose Your Chart Type

This is where most people mess up. They start with the data instead of starting with the question.

Here's what you need to ask yourself:

What story am I trying to tell?

  • Are you comparing things? (Bar charts, column charts)

  • Are you showing change over time? (Line charts, area charts)

  • Are you displaying parts of a whole? (Pie charts, donut charts)

  • Are you showing relationships? (Scatter plots, bubble charts)

Who is my audience?

  • Are they data people or regular folks?

  • How much time do they have to look at this?

  • What level of detail do they need?

What action do I want them to take?

  • Should they investigate something?

  • Do they need to make a decision?

  • Are you just informing them?

Once you answer these questions, the right chart type becomes obvious.

Step 2: Check Your Initial Format (This Changes Everything)

Now here's something most people never think about: the format of your data matters way more than you think.

Look at your spreadsheet. Really look at it. Is it set up in a way that makes building your chart easy, or are you about to fight with your tool for the next hour?

Good data format looks like this:

  • One row per observation

  • Clear column headers

  • No merged cells or fancy formatting

  • Missing data handled properly

  • Consistent data types in each column

Bad data format looks like this:

  • Summary tables with totals mixed in

  • Multiple variables crammed into one column

  • Inconsistent naming (Jan, January, 01)

  • Colors and formatting doing the work that data should do

If your data isn't chart-ready, fix it now. Seriously. Don't try to work around bad formatting. It always comes back to bite you later.

Pro tip: If you find yourself doing weird tricks to make your chart work, your data probably isn't formatted right.

Step 3: Create Calculated Fields & Test Your Logic

This step separates the good analysts from the great ones.

Most people take their raw data and chart it directly. But raw data rarely tells the story you want to tell. You usually need to calculate something first.

Common calculated fields you might need:

  • Percentages (what portion of total sales came from each region?)

  • Growth rates (how much did we grow month over month?)

  • Running totals (what's our cumulative progress toward the goal?)

  • Averages or medians (what's typical performance?)

  • Ratios (how efficient are we getting?)

But here's the key part: test your calculations before you build the chart.

Make sure the numbers make sense. Check your math. Verify that your percentages add up to 100% when they should.

Step 4: Build Your Chart

Okay, now you get to do the fun part. But even here, there's a right way and a wrong way.

Start simple. Don't add every bell and whistle your tool offers. Build the most basic version of your chart first, then add complexity only if it helps tell your story better.

Focus on the data, not the decorations. Your chart should highlight the important stuff and fade everything else into the background. That means:

  • Make your data stand out with color and size

  • Make your axes and gridlines light and subtle

  • Only label the things that matter

  • Remove any elements that don't add value

Make it readable. Use fonts big enough to read easily. Pick colors that work for colorblind folks. Make sure there's enough contrast.

Step 5: Format Like a Pro

This is where good charts become great charts. The formatting is what makes people want to keep looking and actually understand what you're showing them.

Clean up your axes. Round your numbers to sensible values. If you're showing millions of dollars, don't display 2,847,293. Show 2.8M instead. Your audience will thank you.

Add context. A line that goes up is nice. A line that goes up 23% while the industry average went down 5% is a story. Add reference lines, benchmarks, or targets that help people understand if your numbers are good or bad.

Use color with purpose. Don't make everything rainbow colored just because you can. Use color to highlight what's important. Make the good stuff green and the bad stuff red only if that makes sense. Sometimes gray is your best friend.

Why This Process Actually Works

Look, I know this seems like a lot of steps for "just making a chart." But here's why it works:

You avoid the back-and-forth nightmare. You know how you build a chart, show it to someone, and they immediately ask for something completely different? This process stops that. When you think through requirements first, you build what people actually need.

Your charts tell clear stories. When you start with the story instead of the data, your charts have a point. People look at them and immediately get what you're trying to say.

You save time in the long run. Yes, this takes longer upfront. But you'll spend way less time rebuilding charts and explaining what they mean.

You look like you know what you're doing. When you present a well-thought-out chart that clearly communicates an insight, people notice. This is how you build a reputation as someone who really gets data.

Here's what I want you to do: take your next chart project and try this process. All of it. Don't skip steps because you're in a hurry.

Start with the requirements. Figure out what story you're telling before you touch any tools. Clean up your data format. Test your calculations. Then build and format with purpose.

I promise you'll be surprised at how much better your charts get.

title: 5 Chart Types You're Probably Using Wrong
subtitle: Stop misleading your audience with these common visualization errors
body_html:
Some chart mistakes just won’t go away. No matter how many times people see them fail, they keep coming back.

Maybe it’s because they look familiar. Maybe it’s because most people just copy whatever chart they saw last.

But these mistakes do real damage. They lead to the wrong insights. They waste your audience’s time. And they make you look less prepared than you are.

Let’s go over five common chart types that often cause more harm than good, and what to use instead.

1. The Pie Chart: When Parts Don't Add Up

Pie charts look simple, but they cause a lot of problems. You should only use pie charts when your data adds up to 100%. But people often use them to compare things that don't relate to each other.

Even when you use pie charts correctly, they're hard to read. Our eyes can't compare slice sizes very well. This makes your audience guess instead of understanding your data clearly.

Use a Bar Chart instead

Bar charts work much better. It's easy to compare the length of different bars. You can use them for sales numbers, survey results, or budget breakdowns. Bars make your data clear and easy to understand.

If you must show parts of a whole, use only 5-6 pieces. Make sure they add up to 100%.

2. The Dual-Axis Chart: Making Fake Connections

Dual-axis charts put two different types of data on one chart. They have one scale on the left side and another on the right side. This might save space, but it creates big problems.

You can change the scales to make unrelated data look connected. For example, you could make ice cream sales and car accidents look related by adjusting the numbers. But they're not actually connected, both just happen more in summer.

This tricks people into seeing relationships that don't exist.

Use Two Separate Charts instead

Make two charts instead of one. Put them side by side. This way, people can see both sets of data without getting confused. Each chart shows its data honestly.

If you want to show how two things relate, use a scatter plot instead.

3. The Stacked Bar Chart: Too Many Layers

The Problem

Stacked bar charts can show how a total breaks into pieces. But they get confusing when you have more than 2-3 categories. The middle and top sections are hard to compare because they don't start from the same place.

People can compare the bottom sections easily because they all start at zero. But the other sections float at different heights, making comparisons impossible.

Use a Grouped Bar Chart instead

Put each category side by side instead of stacking them. This gives every category its own starting point at zero. People can compare all the categories easily.

4. The Line Chart: Connecting Things That Don't Connect

Line charts are great for showing changes over time. But people often use them wrong. They connect separate categories that have nothing to do with each other.

When you draw lines between different products or departments, you suggest they're connected in order. This confuses people and makes them see trends that don't exist.

Use a Bar Chart instead

For separate categories, use bar charts. Each bar stands alone, which shows that your categories are independent. Use bars for comparing sales, survey scores, or costs across different groups.

Save line charts for data that changes over time.

5. The Heatmap: Rainbow Mess

Heatmaps show patterns using colors. But many people use rainbow colors or bright, clashing colors. This creates confusion instead of clarity.

Rainbow colors are especially bad because they don't show a clear order. Is green higher than blue? People can't tell, so they miss the real patterns in your data.

Bright colors also grab attention even when the data isn't important. This misleads people about what matters most.

Use One Color from Light to Dark instead

Pick one color and make it lighter for low values and darker for high values. Blue, green, or gray work well. This makes it obvious which numbers are high and which are low.

How to Make the Change

You don't need expensive software to make better charts. You can fix most of these problems in Excel, Google Sheets, or PowerPoint.

The key is to think before you make each chart. Ask yourself: "What do I want people to understand from this data?" Then pick the chart that shows that story most clearly.

Before you create any chart, think about your main message. Then choose the chart type that delivers that message in the clearest way possible.

title: The Simple Trick That Makes Your Data 10x Clearer
subtitle: Why the order of your data matters more than the data itself
body_html:
Our brains are wired to find patterns.

When data is randomly thrown together, your audience has to work extra hard to understand what you're trying to say.

That's extra work nobody wants

But when your data flows in a logical way, something magical happens. People "get it" faster.

That's the power of smart ordering. It guides people's eyes exactly where you want them to look.

The Big Three Ordering Strategies

1. Highest to Lowest (The Ranking Story)

This one's a crowd favorite. When you sort from biggest to smallest, you're basically saying "here's what matters most."

Perfect for:

  • Sales by region

  • Website traffic sources

  • Customer complaints by category

  • Budget spending by department

People love rankings. We rank everything from movies to restaurants. Your brain instantly knows that the top item is the winner.

Tip: Sometimes lowest to highest works better. Like showing response times or error rates. You want the smallest bar to be the winner.

2. Time Order (The Change Story)

This is where you show how things move over time. It's like watching a movie of your data.

Perfect for:

  • Monthly sales trends

  • User growth over quarters

  • Daily website visits

  • Seasonal patterns

Time is something everyone understands. We all live in it. When you show data over time, people can relate it to their own experiences.

Tip: Pick your time chunks wisely. Daily data for a year is way too much. Monthly or quarterly usually hits the sweet spot.

3. Logical Order (The Natural Flow Story)

Some things just have a natural order that makes sense. Like steps in a process or stages in a journey.

Perfect for:

  • Education levels (high school → college → graduate)

  • Age groups (18-25, 26-35, 36-45, etc.)

  • Customer journey stages (awareness → consideration → purchase)

  • Project phases (planning → building → testing → launch)

Your audience doesn't have to think about the order. It just feels right.

Tip: If you're not sure about the logical flow, ask yourself "what comes next?" If there's an obvious answer, you've found your logical order.

Quick Decision Framework

If you are stuck on ordering, use these questions

  1. Am I showing performance or comparison? ⇒ Use ranking (highest to lowest)

  2. Am I showing change or trends? ⇒ Use time order

  3. Does this follow a natural sequence? ⇒ Use logical order

Good data ordering isn't about following strict rules. It's about making your audience's job easier.

When people can quickly understand your data, they trust it more. And when they trust your data, they act on it.

Next time you're putting together a chart or report, spend an extra few minutes thinking about order. Your audience will thank you. And you'll look like the data storytelling genius you're becoming.

What's one chart you're working on this week? Let's talk about the best way to order it.

title: The Best Dashboard You’ll Ever Use Has Only 4 Metrics
subtitle: And no, it’s not built in Tableau.
body_html:
Think about your car's dashboard for a second.

It's one of the best examples of clean, effective design.

When you're cruising down the highway at 70 mph, you're not getting bombarded with numbers and charts.

You get exactly what you need:

  • Speed – Are you going too fast or too slow?

  • Fuel – Will you make it to your destination?

  • Engine Temperature – Is something about to go wrong?

  • RPM – Are you pushing the engine too hard?

Four key signals. All designed to help you drive safely and confidently.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts.

Meanwhile, your car has hundreds of sensors measuring everything from tire pressure to AC coolant levels. But do you see all of that while you drive?

Nope.

Because car dashboard designers understood something most data analysts forget:
More information doesn’t mean better decisions.

The Information Overload Problem

Now imagine if your car dashboard looked like most business dashboards. Picture this nightmare scenario:

You're driving to work, and your dashboard is showing:

  • Tire pressure (all four tires, separately)

  • Oil viscosity readings

  • Brake pad thickness measurements

  • Battery voltage levels

  • Wind direction and speed

  • Engine torque output

  • Fuel-to-air mixture ratios

  • Cabin humidity percentage

  • Windshield wiper fluid levels

  • Seat belt tension

  • Radio signal strength

  • GPS satellite connections

It’s too much. You’d probably crash within a mile.

Not because you're a bad driver, but because your brain can only process so much at once.

Why We Mess Up Data Dashboards

So why do we do exactly this with our work dashboards?

Here’s how it usually starts:
Someone says, “We need a dashboard to track sales.”

Sounds simple. But then…

“Can we also add website traffic?”
“What about customer satisfaction scores?”
“Social media mentions too!”
“Oh, and last quarter’s numbers!”
“Maybe weather data? That affects sales!”

Before you know it, your dashboard looks like the control panel of a spaceship.

All that data might be interesting. But is it helping anyone make better decisions?

Usually not.

What Makes Car Dashboards So Effective

Car dashboards are effective because they follow four simple principles:

They prioritize by importance. The speedometer is big and central. The check engine light only appears when something's wrong. Everything has its place based on how critical it is.

They use visual hierarchy. Important stuff is bigger, brighter, or more centrally located. You don't need to hunt for your speed, it's right there in front of you.

They're contextual. Most of the time, you see the basics. But when something needs attention (like low fuel), that information becomes more prominent.

They're scannable. You can check everything you need in about two seconds without taking your eyes off the road for too long.

How to Apply This to Your Dashboards

So how do you make your data dashboards more like car dashboards? Here are some practical steps:

Start with the core question. What's the one most important thing this dashboard needs to answer? That's your speedometer. Everything else is secondary.

Use the 5-second rule. Someone should be able to look at your dashboard and understand the current situation in five seconds or less. If they can't, you've got too much going on.

Group related information. Just like car dashboards group engine-related warnings together, group your related metrics. Don't scatter similar information all over the place.

Make status clear. Use colors, icons, and visual cues to show whether things are good, bad, or need attention.

Hide the details. Not everything needs to be visible all the time. Let people drill down into details when they need them, but keep the main view clean.

The hardest part of building better dashboards isn’t technical. It’s mental.

It’s the ability to not show everything.
To trust that clarity beats completeness.
To design with purpose, not panic.

Remember, the goal isn't to show off how much data you can collect.

The goal is to help people make better decisions, faster.

title: The Dirty Secret Every Senior Analyst Knows (But Won't Tell You)
subtitle: What to do before you clean a single cell.
body_html:
Data doesn't just appear. Humans create it.

And humans are weird, lazy, creative, and unpredictable.

That means every dataset you open is a mirror.

Not just of business processes, but of human behavior, pressure, habits, and workarounds. Clean it too fast, and you risk scrubbing away the most important clues.

This is the side of data work nobody talks about in tutorials.

The part that feels more like psychology than Python.

Let’s get into it.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

In a sales dataset, if all the missing commission amounts belong to one manager, that's not a data quality issue. That's either a problem with their reporting system or they're hiding something.

If survey responses are missing for specific age groups, that's not random. That's telling you something about how those people interact with your survey method.

If timestamps cluster around certain hours, that's revealing when people actually use your product vs. when you think they do.

The pattern in what's NOT there is just as important as what IS there.

That person who bought 847 units of your product. Don't remove them. Find them. They might be running a business you didn't know existed.

Those users with session times of 14 hours. They're not errors. They're power users who left your app open, which tells you something important about your product's stickiness.

The Psychology of Data Generation

What we call data is just a reflection of how humans think, act, skip steps, and make things up on the fly.

People Lie to Forms

Not maliciously, but they do. They put fake ages, round numbers, and give socially acceptable answers. Your cleaning process should expect this, not fix it.

When you see a bunch of ages ending in 0 or 5, that's not random rounding. That's people being vague on purpose. Ask yourself why they don't want to be precise.

People Game the System

If you're measuring sales performance, watch how the data changes near month-end. If you're tracking website engagement, see what happens right before reviews. The "messy" spikes aren't data errors, they're human behavior.

Those weird submission times at 11:58 PM on the last day of the month is not a system glitch. That's someone trying to hit their quota.

People Work Around Broken Systems

When I see text like "see notes field" in a number column, I don't just convert it to null. I go find the notes field. Someone was trying to tell me something important that didn't fit in your neat little database schema.

That creative use of the "other" category is someone's telling you your options are incomplete.

The Questions Nobody Asks

Instead of "How do I clean this data?" ask:

  • "What was the person entering this data thinking?"

  • "What business rule created this weird pattern?"

  • "Who benefits if I clean this vs. keep it messy?"

  • "What story does the mess tell that the clean data hides?"

  • "Am I cleaning this because it's wrong, or because it's inconvenient?"

The most dangerous question in data analysis is "How do I make this cleaner?" The most valuable question is "Why is this messy?"

Your New Data Cleaning Philosophy

Stop trying to make your data perfect. Start trying to make your data honest.

Clean with purpose, not perfection. Every cleaning decision should serve your analysis goal. Don't clean just to clean.

Question the clean data as much as the messy data. If something looks too perfect, it probably is. Real-world data has rough edges.

Talk to the humans. The person who enters the data knows more about what's wrong with it than your computer does.

Preserve the context. Don't just fix values. Document what they were before you fixed them and why they were that way.

The best data analysts aren't the ones with the cleanest datasets. They're the ones who understand why their data is messy and use that messiness to find insights others miss.

Because at the end of the day, perfect data tells you what you want to hear. Messy data tells you what you need to know.

And that's the difference between being a data janitor and being a data detective.

Which one do you want to be?

title: Nobody Reads Your Full Report. Here's Why That's Okay
subtitle: How to help decision makers focus on what matters most
body_html:
Sometimes the best thing you can do for your report is to take stuff out of it.

I know, I know.

You spent hours on that analysis.

You found so many interesting patterns.

Your pivot tables are works of art.

But cramming everything into one report is like trying to tell someone your entire life story when they just asked what you did yesterday.

So how do you figure out what should stay and what should go?

Here's the secret weapon that'll save you every time.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Before you include anything in your report, ask yourself: "So what?"

That beautiful chart showing sales by day of the week? So what? Does it change what the business should do?

The correlation you found between website visits and rainfall? So what? Can the company actually use this information?

If you can't answer "so what?" in a way that connects to business goals, maybe it doesn't belong in your report.

Now that you know the test to use, let's talk about what usually doesn't pass it.

Common Things That Can Go

1. Every Single Chart You Made

You probably created 20 charts while exploring the data. Your report doesn't need all 20. Pick the 3-5 that tell the clearest story.

Focus on the chart that shows the main trend everyone needs to see.

Skip the chart that shows the same trend from a slightly different angle.

2. All Your Data Cleaning Steps

Your boss doesn't need to know that you spent two hours fixing date formats. Save that for your documentation, not your report.

A simple note like "Data covers January 2024 to March 2024, with 95% completeness" works much better than "First, I imported the CSV file, then I noticed 47 rows had incorrect date formats, so I used the DATEVALUE function to convert..."

3. Statistical Jargon That Doesn't Help

Your audience probably doesn't care about p-values, confidence intervals, or R-squared unless they specifically asked for them.

"Sales increased by 15% this quarter" hits harder than "The linear regression model shows an R-squared of 0.847 with a p-value less than 0.05."

4. Every Possible Breakdown

Yes, you can slice the data by region, department, product, time period, customer type, and weather conditions. But should you?

Stick to the breakdowns that reveal actionable insights.

Skip the breakdowns you created just because you could.

5. Obvious Findings

Don't waste space telling people things they already know.

"Holiday sales peaked in December, but this year's peak was 30% higher than last year" is much more valuable than just "Holiday sales peaked in December."

How to Decide What Stays

1. Start With the End Goal

What decision is this report supposed to help make? What problem is it solving? Everything in your report should connect back to this goal.

2. Know Your Audience

Are you presenting to executives who want the big picture? Or analysts who need the details? Different audiences need different levels of information.

For executives: Focus on the business impact and recommended actions

For analysts: Include more methodology and detailed findings

For operations teams: Emphasize actionable insights they can implement

3. Use the Pyramid Principle

Start with your main conclusion. Then add the supporting points. Then add the details if needed.

Think of it like a news article. The headline gives you the main point. The first paragraph gives you the key details. The rest of the article gives you the full story.

4. The "Appendix Test"

If you're not sure whether something belongs in the main report, ask: "Would this be better in an appendix?"

Details about data sources, methodology notes, and extra charts often work better as appendices. This keeps your main report focused while still providing backup information for people who want it.

When Detail Actually IS Important

Now, I've been pretty harsh about cutting things out, but sometimes you do need to include more detail:

  • When your audience specifically asked for it

  • When the methodology affects the reliability of your findings

  • When there are important caveats or limitations

  • When you're documenting something for future reference

  • When the detail changes the recommended action

The key is being intentional about what you include and why.

Great reports aren't about showing everything you found. They're about showing what matters most in the clearest way possible.

Your job as a data analyst isn't just to analyze data.

It's to turn data into insights that drive action.

And sometimes, the best way to drive action is to leave things out.

So next time you're tempted to include that extra chart or detailed explanation, ask yourself: "Does this help my reader make a better decision?"

If the answer is no, it's probably time to hit the delete button.

Your future self (and your readers) will thank you for it.

What's the hardest thing for you to leave out of your reports? Drop a comment and let's discuss how to make our reports more focused and impactful!

title: The Difference Between Data Reporting and Data Storytelling
subtitle: Why your analysis isn't getting attention (and how to fix it)
body_html:
Most people don’t understand data. And they don’t have time to figure it out.

That’s why they need you.

You’re the translator. You’re the guide. You’re the person who makes sense of it all.

And when you do that well, people notice. They trust you.

They ask for your input. They see you as more than just someone who runs reports.

They see you as someone who drives decisions.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Most data analysts think they’re telling stories with their data.

But they’re not. They’re just reporting numbers.

And there’s a huge difference between the two.

If you want to stand out as a data analyst, you need to know how to turn boring reports into powerful stories that people actually care about.

Let me show you how.

What Is Data Reporting?

Data reporting is when you share what happened. You show the facts. You list the numbers. You say things like:

  • “Sales were 50k in January, 48k in February, and 52k in March.”

  • “Product A sold 200 units. Product B sold 150 units.”

  • “Region 1 performed at 95% of target.”

It’s clean and accurate, but nobody knows what to do with it.

Reporting tells people WHAT happened. But it doesn’t tell them WHY it happened or WHAT TO DO about it.

That’s where storytelling comes in.

What Is Data Storytelling?

Data storytelling takes those same numbers and adds meaning to them. It explains why they matter. It shows the impact. It gives people a reason to care.

Here’s what storytelling sounds like:

“Sales have been steady for three months, but we have a hidden problem. Product B is declining every single month because customers are choosing our competitors who offer faster shipping. If we don’t fix our delivery speed soon, we’ll lose 20% more customers by the end of the year.”

See the difference?

Same data. Completely different message.

Storytelling doesn’t just show the numbers. It connects the dots. It explains what’s really going on. It makes people pay attention.

The Key Differences Between Reporting and Storytelling

Let’s break it down even more:

  • Reporting gives facts. Storytelling gives meaning.

  • Reporting shows numbers. Storytelling shows impact.

  • Reporting says “what.” Storytelling says “so what.”

  • Reporting leaves people confused. Storytelling leaves people ready to act.

How to Turn Your Reporting Into Storytelling

You don’t need to be a creative writer to tell good stories with data. You just need to follow a few simple steps.

1. Start with the problem or question

Don’t start with the data. Start with why the data matters.

What problem are you solving? What question are you answering? What decision needs to be made?

This gives your audience a reason to care from the very beginning.

2. Show the data (but keep it simple)

Now you can bring in your numbers. But don’t overdo it.

Pick the most important metrics. Use clear visuals. Make it easy to understand at a glance.

Remember: less is more. You’re not trying to impress people with fancy charts. You’re trying to make a point.

3. Explain what it means

This is the part most people skip. And it’s the most important part.

Don’t just show that sales dropped 15%. Explain WHY it dropped. What caused it? What patterns do you see? What’s the bigger picture?

This is where you add context. This is where you connect the dots.

4. Connect it to business goals

Your data should always tie back to something the company cares about.

Is it about increasing revenue? Keeping customers happy? Saving money? Growing market share?

Make that connection clear. Show how your findings impact the things that matter most.

5. Recommend what to do next

This is the final piece. And it’s what separates great analysts from average ones.

Don’t just point out problems. Suggest solutions. Give clear, actionable recommendations.

Should the team launch a new campaign? Change the pricing strategy? Focus on a different customer group? Fix a broken process?

Tell them what to do. That’s what they’re waiting for.

Next time you’re working on an analysis, ask yourself these questions:

  • What does this data actually mean?

  • Why should anyone care about this?

  • What action should we take because of this?

If you can answer those questions clearly, you’re not just reporting anymore.

You’re storytelling.

And that’s when people start listening.

That’s the power of data storytelling. And it’s the skill that will set you apart in your career.

title: Nobody Wants to Hear Bad News, But Here's How to Tell Them Anyway
subtitle: What to do when the data shows something nobody wants to see
body_html:
Nobody wakes up excited to tell their boss that sales tanked, customer satisfaction is in the toilet, or that expensive project they greenlit is a flaming disaster.

But, as a data analyst, delivering bad news is part of the job.

The data doesn’t care about feelings. It just... is.

And sometimes what it is happens to be really, really inconvenient.

The good news is, there’s a way to present bad news that doesn’t end with you becoming the office scapegoat or dodging blame in a heated meeting.

It’s all about how you frame it, what you bring to the table, and whether you leave people with a path forward or just a pile of problems.

Let me show you how.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

1. Start with the Facts, Not Feelings

This is rule number one.

Don’t walk in saying “I have terrible news” or “This is really bad.”

Don’t apologize. Don’t sugarcoat it. Don’t make it dramatic. Just say what the data shows.

Bad way: “Guys, I’m really sorry, but the numbers this quarter are terrible. I know you’re not going to like this...”

Good way: “The data shows our customer retention dropped 15% last quarter.”

The first one makes everyone nervous before you even share the number. The second one is calm, clear, and factual.

When you stay neutral, people stay focused on the problem instead of their emotions.

2. Add Context Immediately

Here’s where most people mess up. They drop the bad news and then just... stop.

“Our retention dropped 15%.” Okay. Why?

Context is everything.

When you explain why something happened, people understand. They see the bigger picture. They realize it’s not random or mysterious.

Without context: “Customer retention dropped 15% last quarter.”

With context: “Customer retention dropped 15% last quarter, primarily because our main competitor lowered prices by 20% and we didn’t respond.”

Now people get it.

It’s not because your team failed. It’s not because your product is bad. It’s because something specific happened in the market.

3. Show You Investigated Thoroughly

This step builds trust.

When you present bad news, people want to know: did you actually do the work? Or are you just showing me one chart and guessing?

Prove that you dug deep.

Show them you analyzed the data from multiple angles. That you looked at trends over time. That you compared it to benchmarks or competitors.

Example: “I looked at 500 customer exit surveys, analyzed purchasing patterns across 3 years, and compared our numbers against industry benchmarks.”

When people see you did the work, they trust your conclusions. And that makes them more willing to listen to your recommendations.

4. Present Options, Not Just Problems

Here’s a rule I live by: Never show a problem without showing potential solutions.

Never.

When you dump bad news on people without giving them options, you create helplessness. People feel stuck. They don’t know what to do.

But when you show options, you turn the conversation from “what’s wrong” to “what should we do.”

Example:

“We have three options:

Option A: Match competitor pricing Cost: $X Benefit: Retain customers

Option B: Add value to justify current prices Cost: $Y Benefit: Stand out from competitors

Option C: Do nothing Cost: $Z in lost customers”

Now people have choices.

They can weigh the costs and benefits. They can discuss which path makes the most sense.

5. Recommend a Path Forward

Don’t just list options and walk away. Take a position. Tell them which option you think is best and why.

This is where your expertise matters.

You’re the one who analyzed the data. You’re the one who understands the trends. You’re the one who knows what’s likely to work.

So say it.

Example: “I recommend Option B because our research shows customers value quality over price. 68% of exit surveys mentioned service issues, not cost. If we improve service, we can keep our pricing and still win customers back.”

When you make a clear recommendation backed by data, you make it easier for leaders to decide.

These five steps turn a scary presentation into a productive conversation. But there’s one more thing you need to understand...

Presenting bad news will never be fun. But it doesn’t have to be scary.

When you walk in with solid analysis, clear context, real solutions, and a recommended path forward, you’re not just delivering bad news.

You’re solving problems.

And that’s what good data analysts do.

So next time you have to present something nobody wants to hear, remember to start with the facts, add context, show your work, present options, and recommend a solution.

Do that, and you won’t just survive the meeting. You’ll walk out with people thanking you for catching the problem early.

title: A Million Dollars at a Startup vs. Amazon
subtitle: The same number can mean everything or nothing.
body_html:
“We increased sign-ups by 200%!” sounds like a massive win, right?

Until you find out it went from 2 sign-ups to 6.

Or how about this one: “We added $50 million in revenue!”

Sounds incredible.

Until you learn the company makes $10 billion a year. That’s only a 0.5% increase.

See the problem? Numbers don’t mean anything without context.
