A million dollars matters a lot to a startup. It’s a rounding error to Amazon. And that’s exactly why percentages and absolute numbers can both lie to you.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Problem Most People Don’t Talk About

Percentages and absolute numbers tell completely different stories. And most people, including analysts, managers, and executives, use them wrong.

They either hide behind percentages to make small wins look massive, or they throw out big numbers without context to confuse people.

So let me break down when to use each and become the person in the room who actually understands what the data is saying.

When Percentages Make You Look Silly

Percentages are great for showing relative change. They help you understand growth or decline in relation to where you started.

But here’s the catch: percentages amplify small numbers and hide context from big ones.

Example: The Misleading Small Base

Let’s say you’re running a new marketing campaign.

  • Week 1: You got 2 sign-ups

  • Week 2: You got 6 sign-ups

You could say: “We increased sign-ups by 200%!”

Technically true. But also... meaningless. You went from 2 people to 6 people. That’s not really a breakthrough.

When your starting number is tiny, percentages make everything look like a miracle. But in reality, you haven’t proven anything yet.

Don’t use percentages when your base number is small. You’ll look like you’re trying too hard to impress people, and anyone who knows data will see right through it.

When Absolute Numbers Betray You

Now let’s flip it. Absolute numbers show you the actual magnitude of change. They’re concrete. They’re what actually happened.

But they also hide scale. And scale is everything.

Example: The “Big Number, Small Deal” Illusion

Imagine your company made $50 million more this year than last year.

Sounds amazing, right? $50 million is a LOT of money.

But what if your company makes $10 billion a year? That $50 million is only a 0.5% increase. That’s basically flat. That’s a problem.

A million dollars matters a lot to a startup. It’s a rounding error to Amazon.

So When Should You Use Each?

Here’s the simple rule I follow:

Use Percentages When:

  1. You’re comparing things of different sizes. Percentages let you compare apples to oranges (or businesses of different scales).

  2. You want to show growth rates. If you’re tracking performance over time, percentages show the speed of change.

  3. Your base number is large enough to matter. If you’re starting with at least 100-1,000 data points (depending on context), percentages start making sense.

  4. You want to normalize data. Percentages help you say “this is how big this is relative to the whole.”

Use Absolute Numbers When:

  1. You need to show real-world impact. Revenue, costs, users, and headcount should almost always include absolute numbers.

  2. You’re starting from small numbers. If your base is tiny, absolute numbers keep you honest.

  3. You want to highlight magnitude. When the actual size of the change matters (like budget cuts or revenue gains), lead with the dollar amount.

  4. You’re dealing with executives who care about outcomes. CEOs and CFOs care about actual dollars, not just percentages.

The Best Answer? Use BOTH

Here’s the real secret: the best analysts don’t pick one or the other. They use both, together, in context.

Instead of saying:

“Sales increased 50%”

Say:

“Sales increased 50%, from $100K to $150K”

Instead of saying:

“We added $50M in revenue”

Say:

“We added $50M in revenue, a 5% increase over last year’s $1B”

Now you’re giving the full picture. You’re showing the rate of change AND the actual impact.

Don’t Be the Person Who Uses Numbers Wrong

Be the analyst who gives people the full story. The one who uses percentages when they make sense and absolute numbers when they matter. The one who combines both when needed.

Because data is only useful if people understand it.

And understanding comes from context, not just from picking the number that makes you look best.

So next time someone tells you “sales increased 50%” or “we grew by $50,” you’ll know exactly what question to ask:

“Okay, but what’s the other number?”

That’s when the real story starts.

title: You Don't Need All the Answers to Be a Great Analyst
subtitle: The smartest analysts aren’t always sure
body_html:
Every data project has uncertainty. Trust me, every single one does.


Your sample might be small. Your data might have gaps. The future might not act like the past. People might change. Your model might miss something important.

This isn’t failure. It’s reality.

The best analysts know this and talk about it openly. And people trust them MORE, not less.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Imagine two analysts giving forecasts:

Analyst A: “Sales will rise by 23% next quarter.”
Analyst B: “Based on current trends, sales should rise between 18% and 28% next quarter. That assumes our marketing spend stays steady and no major market changes happen.”

Who sounds more trustworthy? Analyst B does. Because they’re honest about what they know and what they don’t.

Okay, So How Do You Actually Do It?

1. Use Ranges, Not Exact Numbers

Exact numbers look precise but can mislead.

Instead of: “This campaign will bring in 500 customers.”
Try: “This campaign will likely bring in between 400 and 600 customers, with 500 as our best estimate.”

Ranges make you look smart when the final number lands anywhere inside them.

3. Share Your Confidence Level

Not all predictions are equal. Some rest on strong data. Others are rough guesses.

Say it clearly:
“I’m confident in this estimate because we have three years of solid data.”
Or: “This one’s early since we don’t have much data yet.”

People can handle uncertainty. What they hate is surprise.

4. Admit What You Don’t Know

“Here’s what the data tells us clearly. Here’s what’s less certain. And here’s what we don’t know yet.”

This makes you sound honest, not unsure.

5. Show Scenarios

Offer a few possible outcomes.

“If things go well, we’ll see X. If things stay steady, expect Y. If things drop, it could be Z.”

That helps others prepare and shows you’ve thought it through.

What to Say When You Really Don’t Know

Sometimes you simply don’t have enough data. Maybe the sample is too small or the situation is new.

Here’s how to handle that:

Be direct: “I don’t have enough data to answer that confidently.”
Explain why: “We’ve only seen 15 customers in this group, not enough for solid trends.”
Offer options: “I can show what we have and note what more we’d need. I can also check similar groups for clues.”
Set a timeline: “If we track this for another three months, we’ll have enough to say more.”

You’re showing you’re careful and thoughtful.

The Main Thing to Remember

Data is never perfect, so strong analysts don’t pretend they can predict everything.

They face ambiguity with clarity, explain what’s known and unknown, and still give useful insights.

Admitting uncertainty isn’t weakness.

It makes your work more credible. And it’s how you earn lasting trust as an analyst.

title: Everyone's Posting Dashboards, But Nobody's Getting Hired
subtitle: What hiring managers really want to see in your data projects
body_html:
You can post dashboards, get tons of likes, and receive great feedback. It feels awesome.

But then you start applying for jobs and realize... something’s missing.

Do you want to be a Data Analyst or a BI Analyst?

Because building dashboards is just one part of the story. Understanding what each role really does is the key to leveling up your career.

I’m not saying dashboards are bad.

They’re actually pretty awesome. But if you think a portfolio full of pretty charts is going to land you that data analyst job, we need to talk.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Why Is Everyone Obsessed with Dashboards?

There’s a reason dashboard portfolios are everywhere:

They look great. A colorful dashboard grabs attention faster than any table or code.

They’re easy to share. One screenshot on LinkedIn and boom, instant attention.

The tools are beginner-friendly. Tableau and Power BI help you make pretty charts fast. You don’t need to be a coding genius.

Courses push them hard. Almost every data bootcamp or online course has a whole module on visualization. Some make it seem like dashboards are the entire job.

Everyone else is doing it. You see someone get 500 likes on a dashboard. You think, ‘I need to do that too.’

None of this is bad.

Dashboards ARE important. And yes, being able to present data in a clear, visual way is part of many data jobs.

But, the truth is, a dashboard alone doesn’t prove you can analyze data. It just shows you can use a tool.

What’s Missing From Most Dashboard Portfolios?

Most people show you the final dashboard. But they don’t show you the work that happened BEFORE the dashboard. And that’s exactly what hiring managers want to see.

Let me break it down.

Showing Your Thinking

When you only show a dashboard, people can’t see:

How did you decide what to analyze? What question were you trying to answer? Why does this analysis matter?

Most dashboards don’t answer any of these questions. They just show charts.

Showing the Messy Work

Making charts is the LAST step. But what about everything before that?

Where did the data come from? Was it messy? What SQL queries did you write? Did you work with multiple datasets?

If your portfolio doesn’t show this, you’re hiding the most important part of your work.

Showing What You Found

This is where a lot of people fall short. They make the chart, but they don’t explain what the chart MEANS.

What patterns did you find? Were there any surprises? What would you recommend based on your findings? What questions would you ask next?

Most dashboard posts stop at “here’s a chart.” They don’t dig into what the chart is telling you.

So... Data Analyst or BI Analyst?

Here’s where things get interesting. Both roles use dashboards. But they use them for different reasons.

You might be a BI Analyst if:

You love dashboards because:

  • You enjoy design and making things look good and function smoothly

  • You like building tools that others will use every day

  • You want to work with BI tools like Tableau, Power BI, or Looker most of the day

  • You prefer structure and creating repeatable processes

  • You like maintaining systems and making sure reports run on schedule

  • You enjoy working with existing data models and making them easy to use

If this sounds like you, BI roles might be perfect. There’s nothing wrong with that. BI Analysts are valuable and needed.

You might be a Data Analyst if:

You love dashboards because:

  • They help you show what you discovered after digging through data

  • They’re the final step after all the analysis work is done

  • You want to answer “why” questions and figure out what’s really happening

  • You enjoy exploring data and finding insights no one asked for yet

  • You like solving business problems with data, not just displaying it

  • You want to figure out and understand the story behind the numbers

If this sounds more like you, then Data Analyst roles are probably your path. And that means your portfolio needs to show MORE than just dashboards.

Neither role is better than the other. They’re just different. And knowing which one you’re drawn to will help you build the right skills and apply to the right jobs.

Dashboards Aren’t the Enemy

Let me be clear about something.

Dashboards are NOT bad. They’re useful. They’re fun to build. They look good on your portfolio.

But they’re ONE piece of a much bigger puzzle.

The analysts who actually get hired aren’t just dashboard builders. They’re people who can:

Think critically about problems. Work with messy, real data. Find insights that matter. Explain what they found in simple words. Make recommendations that businesses can actually use

That’s what separates you from everyone else posting pretty charts.

So yes, build your dashboards. Make them look great. Share them online.

But also show the work behind them. Show your thinking. Show the mess. Show the questions you asked and the answers you found.

Because THAT’S what proves you’re ready for the job.

And that’s what’s going to get you hired.

title: I’ve Got Some Good News and Bad News.
subtitle: The psychology behind good news, bad news storytelling
body_html:
I’ve got some good news and bad news.

Good news: I hit 40 subscribers on my newsletter last month!

Bad news: That’s also the exact number of my cousins, aunts, uncles, and close friends combined. 🫣

The good news tells me people who know me are willing to support. The bad news tells me I haven’t figured out how to reach anyone beyond my family and friends yet.

It means I have support, but not yet an audience.

See what just happened there?

You probably paid more attention to those few lines than you would to most data charts.

Your brain locked in. You wanted to know where this was going.

That’s the power of the “good news, bad news” structure.

And it works just as well when you’re presenting data at work.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Why This Simple Trick Works So Well

People are ready to hear “good news, bad news.”

We’ve been hearing it our whole lives. In movies. From our parents. From our bosses. It’s baked into how we expect information to be delivered when there’s both progress and problems.

So when you use this structure, you’re not making people learn a new way to think. You’re tapping into something they already know.

And that makes everything easier.

Here’s an example. Imagine you’re presenting quarterly results to your team.

You could dump a bunch of numbers on them. Show them charts. Make them work to figure out what’s happening.

Or you could do this:

“I have good news and bad news.

Good news: We acquired 500 new customers last quarter. Most ever.

Bad news: We lost 600 customers. Also most ever.

The good news is we’re getting better at acquiring customers. The bad news is we’re getting worse at keeping them.

Net result: We shrunk by 100 customers despite record acquisition.

Here’s what we need to do...”

See the difference?

The structure shows the full picture without overwhelming anyone. It tells a complete story in a way people can actually follow.

And most importantly, it naturally leads to action. “Here’s what we need to do” feels like the obvious next step, not some random change of topic.

But Wait, There’s a Twist

Most people (like 78% according to research) prefer to hear bad news first, then good news. It feels nicer. It’s the classic “softening the blow” approach. You end on a high note, everyone leaves feeling okay about life.

But here’s the twist that changed how I present data: nicer isn’t always better.

Start With Good, End With Bad

This is your power move when you need people to actually do something.

Why? Because the bad news sticks. It lingers in their mind after the conversation ends. They walk out of that meeting thinking “we need to fix this NOW.” It creates urgency.

Think about my newsletter example. I led with the good news (40 subscribers), then hit you with the reality (they’re all family). What are you thinking about right now? Probably the fact that I need to actually grow this thing beyond my cousin Alex.

That’s not an accident. That’s psychology working for you.

When to use it:

  • Presenting to decision makers who need to approve budget

  • Any situation where the goal is “get people to act”

  • Client reports where you need them to take your recommendations seriously

The good news hooks them in and makes them receptive. The bad news sends them out the door ready to solve problems.

Start With Bad, End With Good

This is your relationship move. It’s gentler. It’s kinder. People genuinely prefer it because you’re ending on a positive note.

When to use it:

  • Team updates and casual stand-ups

  • Sharing results that are disappointing but not critical

  • Any time you’re NOT asking for immediate action

The bad news gets processed first, then the good news acts like a buffer. It’s the emotional reset that helps people leave feeling okay.

How I Decide Which Order to Use

Here’s how I think about it in real situations:

Use good news first when you’re presenting to decision makers or trying to get budget approved. End with the problem so they leave thinking about solutions.

Use bad news first when you’re giving updates to your team or in casual conversations. End with hope so they stay motivated.

Both work. You just need to pick the right tool for the job.

Real Examples You Can Steal Right Now

Example 1: Website Performance

“I have good news and bad news about our website.

Good news: Page load time is down to 2 seconds. That’s lightning fast.

Bad news: Bounce rate is up 25%.

The good news means our tech team did amazing work on speed. The bad news means speed isn’t our problem. Something else is making people leave.

Net result: We fixed the wrong thing. We need to look at our content and layout instead.

Here’s what I recommend: Let’s run user tests next week to see where people actually get confused.”

Example 2: Email Campaign

“I have good news and bad news about last week’s email.

Bad news: Only 12% of people opened it. That’s below our usual 18%.

Good news: Of the people who opened it, 35% clicked through. That’s double our normal rate.

The bad news means our subject line didn’t work. The good news means our email content was fire once people actually read it.

Net result: Great email, terrible packaging.

Here’s the fix: Let’s A/B test three new subject lines for the next campaign and keep the same content style.”

The Only Thing You Need To Remember

The “good news, bad news” structure works because people already know it. You’re not teaching them a new way to think. You’re using a pattern that’s already living in their head.

That’s smart communication. That’s what good data storytelling looks like.

So next time you’re staring at a dashboard full of mixed results, ask yourself three questions:

  1. What’s the good news?

  2. What’s the bad news?

  3. What do I want people to do about it?

Then tell them. In whatever order makes sense for your goal.

Just like my subscriber count situation. Sure, those 40 people might be family and friends. But at least they understood exactly where things stand.

And now, so do you.

title: The Gift and Risk of Data Storytelling
subtitle: One simple number can tell three very different truths
body_html:
You look at a dashboard and see this:

Conversion rate this month: 5.0 percent
Conversion rate last month: 4.5 percent

Nice. It went up.

But what does that really mean?

  • A marketer might say, “The new campaign is working.”

  • A product manager might say, “Users are finding the value faster.”

  • A finance lead might say, “Revenue is growing.”

  • A support lead might say, “Tickets will go up again.”

All of them are reacting to the same metric.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

This is why one metric can feel powerful and confusing at the same time. The number is fixed. The story around it is not.

The good news is that you can use this on purpose. You can shape the story to fit the audience and the decision.

To show this, let us walk through three stories for the same conversion rate.

Let us use one simple example

This month, the site has 10,000 visitors.
The conversion rate from visitor to paid plan is 5 percent.
That means 500 people buy the product this month.

Last month, the conversion rate was 4.5 percent, so about 450 people bought.

Now we will tell three stories:

  1. A user story

  2. A money story

  3. An operations story

As you read, notice how each one feels different, even though the number is the same.

Story 1: The user story

This story looks at the people behind the metric. It cares about what they see, where they get stuck, and how the product feels.

You might say:

“Out of every 100 visitors, 5 end up paying for our product. So 95 people come, look around, and leave without buying. Our job is to understand why those 95 drop off.”

The metric now becomes a signal of user experience, not just a score.

The same metric supports a story like this:

“Our conversion rate is 5 percent, but it is not only a win. It is also a mirror that shows how many visitors we fail to help. If we fix the sign up flow and make our value clearer in the first 30 seconds, we can raise this number by making the experience better, not just by shouting louder in ads.”

Use this story when you talk with UX designers, product managers, and customer support. They care about friction and want to know where users are struggling.

Story 2: The money story

Now we tell a story for someone who cares about money first. It connects the metric to dollars and growth.

We keep the same numbers:

10,000 visitors. 5 percent conversion rate. That is 500 paying customers. Each pays 20 dollars per month.

So this flow brings in 10,000 dollars per month.

Now ask a simple “what if”:

“If we move conversion from 5 percent to 6 percent with the same traffic, what happens”

At 6 percent, you get 600 customers.

600 times 20 dollars is 12,000 dollars per month. That is 2,000 dollars more every month, from only one extra customer out of 100 visitors.

Now the story sounds like this:

“Our 5 percent conversion rate is good, but each extra 1 percent point is worth about 2,000 dollars in monthly revenue at our current size. If we invest in improving this flow, we are not only being nice to users. We are also unlocking a clear, trackable revenue lever.”

Use this story with executives, investors, and business owners. They want to see how this metric affects growth and profit.

Story 3: The operations story

Now we look at the same metric with an operations view. It is about systems and capacity.

We reuse the numbers:

500 new paying customers in a month. Support team of 3 people. On average, 1 out of 3 new customers opens at least one ticket in the first month.

So this month you get about 165 tickets from new customers.

If next month you push conversion to 7 percent, that is 700 new customers.
One third of 700 is about 230 tickets.

Now the story sounds like this:

“Our conversion rate is rising, which is great for growth, but each bump in conversion also adds more demand on support and onboarding. If we reach 7 percent without better self help content or more staff, our queue will grow by around 40 percent. That means slower replies and more frustrated customers.”

In this story, you are not saying “stop growing.” You are saying:

“If we plan to push this number higher, we must grow our systems with it. Let us improve our knowledge base and maybe add one more support person once we hit 6 percent.”

Use this story with operations managers, data analysts, and people who run the day to day systems. They care about service levels and workload.

None of these stories is a lie

Here is the key idea.

One metric can support many stories. That is the gift and the risk.

All three stories are true.
The user story shows where people struggle. The money story shows the revenue lever. The operations story shows the load on your system.

If you only tell the money story, you may chase higher conversion and ignore user trust and support load.
If you only tell the user story, you may miss why the company cannot fund your ideas.
If you only tell the operations story, you may slow growth because you fear more demand.

Your job as a data person is to know that many stories exist, pick one to lead with, and still keep the others in mind.

title: The Line Doesn't Always Go Up
subtitle: And that's okay... here's why
body_html:
Apple’s revenue hits crazy highs every holiday season. In early 2024, the company made about 119.6 billion dollars in Q1.

Once the holidays ended, the number dropped to about 90.8 billion in Q2 and then 85.8 billion in Q3.

If you only see the drop, it looks like a failure.

But this pattern repeats every single year. This is the shape of the Apple calendar.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

When you look at any real dataset over time, you will notice something similar. The line never goes straight up.

Sales dip in certain months. Website traffic falls on weekends. Even top companies have slow quarters.

We do not call those failures. We call them patterns. Cycles. Seasons.

So why do we forget this when we stare at our own dashboards?

What’s a “Season” Anyway?

Seasons are changes that show up over and over at the same times.

You see them in everyday life:

  • Ice cream sales drop in December

  • Gym memberships spike in January and fade by March

  • Retail explodes in November and December, then quiets down in January

  • Travel bookings peak before summer and major holidays

None of these are mistakes. They are the natural breathing of human behavior.

The challenge is this: when you look at a dataset for the first time, you do not know what “normal” looks like. So the first dip feels like a crisis because you have no context.

Is It a Failure or a Season?

Here is a practical way to figure out what type of dip you are looking at.

1. Look at Your Historical Data

Start with the past. Pull data from previous years and see if the dip appears again.

Ask:

  • Does it happen around the same time each year?

  • Is the size of the dip similar?

  • How long did it take to bounce back before?

If the pattern repeats, you are looking at a season, not a failure.

2. Check External Factors

Some dips line up with events outside the dashboard.

Think about:

  • Holidays and school schedules

  • Weather changes

  • Industry cycles

  • Cultural moments and big events

If ad clicks crash during the Super Bowl, that is not a failing ad. People are simply watching TV.

3. Compare Against Industry Benchmarks

Do not look at your data alone.

Check:

  • Industry benchmarks

  • Competitor trends

  • Market movement

If everyone dips at the same time, it is likely seasonal.
If only you dip while others grow, that is a red flag.

4. Talk to People Who Know the History

People who have been in the company for years know the rhythm.

You will hear things like:

  • “Q3 is always slow.”

  • “Engagement drops after big launches.”

  • “Sales fall during school exams.”

Mix human memory with your data. It gives you strong context. These insights save you hours of digging through data.

How to Use This in Your Actual Work

Once you spot a seasonal pattern, use it to guide your work.

Build simple baselines.
Look at two to three years of data and note when dips and peaks usually happen. Add key factors like holidays or weather. Even one simple note like ‘Sales fall in Q3 and rise again in Q4’ helps a lot.

Add context to your dashboards.
Never show one number alone. Include last month and the same month last year. A month to month dip looks scary until you see year to year growth.

Annotate your charts.
Add small notes like “Holiday spike” or “School break dip.” This helps everyone understand the pattern without guessing.

Lead with context.
When you present results, start by saying what is normal for that season. Then explain what is new or different. This keeps the focus on insight, not panic.

Let’s Zoom Out for a Second

Data is not just numbers. It reflects human behavior. And human behavior moves in cycles.

People travel. People rest. People follow calendars, weather, and moods.

Not every dip needs a fix. Not every slowdown is a crisis. Many dips are simply seasons.

And when you learn to read those seasons, the data becomes easier to explain and easier to trust.

Your job is not to make every month go up. Your job is to know what is normal, spot what is different, and help people understand why.

title: Stop Making Charts for Everything
subtitle: Here is how to know when a table does the job better.
body_html:
Not every piece of data needs to be visualized

I know, I know. We are always told that visuals are king.

“Make it visual.” “People do not read tables.” “Charts are more engaging.” And yes, most of the time, that is true.

But sometimes a table is exactly what you need.

Let me explain.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Everyone Loves a Good Chart (Maybe Too Much)

If you have spent any time in data, or taken a data bootcamp course, you have heard this idea many times. Charts and graphs are the best way to share insights.

Bar charts, line charts, pie charts (okay, maybe not pie charts), scatter plots. We are trained to reach for a chart first.

Charts are great. They help people see trends at a glance. They make it easy to compare values and spot patterns without reading a lot of text. A good chart can tell a story in a few seconds.

But here is the key point. Charts are not always the answer.

When a Table Beats a Chart

Let us look at the moments where tables shine.

1. When you need exact numbers

Say you are looking at product spending. A bar chart tells you that Wines has the highest spend. Good.

But then someone asks, “How much did we spend on Meat?”

With a table, the answer is easy. They look once and see 165.3 dollars. Done.

With a chart, even with labels, they may squint or guess. That slows them down.

Look at the Product Mix Analysis example. The table is clean and clear. In one glance you see the product name, the average spend, and the percent share.

2. When you have more than one number per row

Now look at the Customer Conversion by Campaign example.

Six campaigns. Two numbers for each one. Accepted Customers and Acceptance Rate.

You could make two charts. One chart for accepted customers. One chart for acceptance rate. Now your reader has to look in two places to understand one idea.

Or you can use a table. Everything is together. Easy to scan. Easy to compare.

3. When your audience wants to dig in

Not every stakeholder wants only a big picture view. Some people like the raw numbers.

Analysts, finance teams, and technical staff often prefer tables. They want to explore the data, cross check values, or copy the numbers into another tool.

For them, a table is not boring. It is useful.

But wait, charts are not bad

I am not against charts. Charts are very valuable. They are great for stories, for trends over time, and for helping non technical people engage with the data.

Most tools now let you add labels to charts with one click. So you can keep the visual punch and still show exact values.

For example, you could turn the Product Mix table into a horizontal bar chart with labels on each bar. You would see the size of each product and also the exact dollar amount.

So charts are not bad at all. They are just not the only option.

It All Comes Down to This

The “table vs chart” debate is not really a fight. It is about picking the right tool for the job.

Ask yourself:

  • What does my audience need right now? A quick picture or exact numbers?

  • What story am I telling? A trend over time or a clear comparison?

  • How will this data be used? Fast decisions or deeper analysis?

If your audience needs to spot patterns fast, use a chart.
If they need exact values and details, use a table.

If they need both, give them both. Put a chart at the top for the story and a table under it for the details.

There is no rule that says you must choose only one.

title: The One Rule That Fixes All Your Formatting Problems
subtitle: If it means the same thing, make it look the same. That's it.
body_html:
We like to think our audience reads our charts like a book.

We think they start at the top, read every label, and look at the data perfectly.

But in reality? They’re skimming.

Your audience is in a hurry. Their eyes move fast. They look for simple patterns they can understand fast.

When you choose a color or a layout, you’re making a silent promise to them. You’re telling them how to read your story.

Here’s why you need to keep that promise.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Silent Promises You’re Making

Every time you make a formatting choice, you’re making a promise to your viewer.

Colors make promises. If blue means “Sales” on your first slide, it can’t suddenly mean “Expenses” on slide three. That’s confusing. That’s breaking trust.

Sorting makes promises. If you sort your first table from highest to lowest, don’t sort your second table alphabetically. Your audience expects things to stay the same. When you change the rules, they get lost.

Labels make promises. If you put your data labels on top of bars in one chart, don’t put them inside the bars in the next chart. Keep it the same.

Layouts make promises. If your KPIs are in the top right corner on one page, they better be in the top right corner on every page.

These are not just design choices. They act like a map. They help people understand your work without thinking too hard.

What Happens When You Break These Promises

When you break your formatting patterns, something bad happens.

Your audience stops listening to your story. They stop thinking about the insights. They stop caring about the numbers.

Instead, their brain starts working hard. They start trying to learn how to read your chart all over again.

“Wait, what does this color mean now?”

“Why is this sorted differently?”

“Where did that label go?”

And while they are busy solving your formatting puzzle, they miss your main point.

When Blue Becomes the Color of Confusion

Let me show you what this looks like in real life.

Slide one shows your top products. Laptops are blue, phones are green, and tablets are orange. You sorted them from highest sales to lowest. Nice and clear.

Then slide two shows your costs. You accidentally make laptops blue again. But this time, blue means money lost, not money made.

Your audience sees the blue bar and thinks, “Great, laptops are doing well again!” Then they read the label and see it’s costs. Their brain gets confused for a moment. They have to stop and relearn what blue means.

That’s one broken promise. If you do this two or three times, people stop trusting your colors. Now they’re reading every single label on every single bar. You’ve turned a quick scan into hard work.

How to Keep Your Promises

The fix is simple. Be consistent.

Pick your colors once. Decide what each color means at the start. Then stick with it.

Pick your sorting once. If you’re sorting by value, always sort by value. If you’re sorting alphabetically, always sort alphabetically.

Pick your layout once. Put your most important numbers in the same spot every time. Your audience should never have to search for information.

Pick your labels once. If you use data labels, use them the same way in every chart. Same position. Same style. Same everything.

Think of it like learning a new language. You cannot change the rules halfway and still expect people to keep up.

The One Rule That Fixes Everything

If you only remember one thing, remember this. If something means the same thing, make it look the same. If it means something different, make it look different.

That’s it. That’s the whole secret.

When blue means sales on page one, blue means sales on page ten. When you sort by dollars on slide two, you sort by dollars on slide twelve.

Your audience is not asking for fancy designs. They’re asking for consistency. They want to learn your system once and then focus on your ideas.

Give them that gift. Keep your silent promises. And watch them actually hear what you’re saying.

Before You Build Your Next Chart

Next time you build a presentation, first spend five minutes on your formatting rules. Do this before you build a single chart. Those five minutes will save you from fifty minutes of confused questions later.

Pick your colors. Pick your sorting style. Pick where your key numbers will go. Write it down if you need to.

Then stick to it.

Your audience will thank you. You will finally get the reaction you want.

title: The Measurement Problem Every Analyst Faces (And How to Fix It)
subtitle: You can't always measure what you want.
body_html:
You want to know if your customers are happy.

But here’s the problem: you can’t just knock on someone’s door and ask, “Hey, on a scale of 1 to 10, how happy are you right now?”

Well, you could 😕, but good luck getting honest answers. People lie. People don’t know how they feel. And most importantly, you can’t do this for thousands of customers every single day.

So what do you do?

You use something called a Proxy Metric.

And if you learn this trick, you can solve a big data problem: how to measure things that feel impossible to measure.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Okay, But What Even Is a Proxy Metric?

A proxy metric is a stand-in. It’s something you can measure that stands for something you can’t measure directly.

Think of it like this:

You want to know if someone is rich. But you can’t see their bank account.

So instead, you look at their car. Their house. Their clothes. These things aren’t money, but they give you clues about money.

That’s a proxy.

In data, we do the same thing.

You want to measure: Customer Happiness

You can’t measure it directly because happiness lives in people’s heads.

So you find a proxy: Maybe it’s how often people come back to buy again (Repeat Purchase Rate). Maybe it’s how long they stay on your website (Time on Site). Maybe it’s how few complaints you get (Support Ticket Volume).

These aren’t happiness. But they leave clues about happiness.

Let Me Show You an Example

Let’s say you run an online store.

You want happy customers. But you can’t read their minds.

So you pick a proxy: Repeat Purchase Rate.

If people keep coming back to buy from you, that’s a good sign they’re happy. If they buy once and never return, that’s a red flag.

Is this perfect? No. But it’s better than nothing.

Another easy example

You sell furniture. You want to know if your furniture is good quality.

You can’t test every single chair and table. That would take forever.

So you pick a proxy: Return Rate.

If people keep sending your stuff back, your quality probably sucks. If almost no one returns anything, you’re doing something right.

Again, not perfect. But useful.

But Wait. There’s a Catch

Proxy metrics are like shadows. They show the rough shape of the real thing. But shadows can look different from the real thing.

Let me explain with an example.

The “Time on Site” Problem

You run a website. You want to know if users are engaged and happy.

So you track Time on Site. More time = more engagement, right?

Not so fast.

Maybe people are spending a long time on your site because they love your content. That’s great!

Or maybe they’re spending a long time on your site because your navigation sucks and they can’t find what they’re looking for. That’s terrible!

Same metric. Opposite meanings.

This is the danger of proxy metrics. They can trick you if you’re not careful.

So How Do You Fix This?

Great analysts find one proxy metric.

Elite analysts use many proxy metrics together to get closer to the truth.

Here’s what that means.

Instead of using only one number, you track several proxies and look for patterns.

Let’s go back to the “Customer Happiness” example.

Triangulating Customer Happiness

You want to know if customers are happy. So you track:

  1. Repeat Purchase Rate (Are they coming back?)

  2. Net Promoter Score (NPS) (Would they recommend you to a friend?)

  3. Average Order Value (Are they buying more over time?)

  4. Support Ticket Volume (Are they complaining?)

  5. Time Between Purchases (How often are they coming back?)

Now you’re not just looking at one shadow. You’re looking at five different shadows from five different angles.

If all five metrics point the same way, you can be pretty sure about what’s happening.

If Repeat Purchase Rate is up, NPS is up, Average Order Value is up, Support Tickets are down, and Time Between Purchases is shrinking, then yeah, your customers are probably happy.

But if Repeat Purchase Rate is up but NPS is down and Support Tickets are spiking, something weird is going on. Maybe people are buying because they have no other option, but they’re not actually happy about it.

That’s triangulation.

You’re using multiple proxies to get closer to the truth.

Here’s What You Need to Remember

You can’t always measure what you want to measure.

But you can find something close.

Find the shadow. Follow the clues. Use more than one proxy to get closer to the truth.

And always remember: You’re not chasing the shadow. You’re chasing the thing that cast it.

That’s the difference between good analysis and great analysis.

That’s the proxy metric trick.

title: Your Chart Can't Explain Itself (But It Should)
subtitle: The simple annotation strategy that makes every chart clearer
body_html:
You won’t always be there to explain your chart.

You might give a great presentation today. But an hour later, your slide deck gets emailed around. Someone opens it on their phone. Someone skims it between meetings. Someone skips your notes and looks straight at the charts.

Will they understand why sales spiked in May? Will they get why traffic dropped in October?

Probably not.

This is where most charts fail. But there is a simple fix: Annotations.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Charts Don’t Explain Themselves

We like to think a clean chart can explain itself. We think good colors and a clear title are enough.

But usually, context is everything.

A line going up looks like success, until you realize it’s counting customer complaints. A sudden drop looks like failure, unless you know a system outage caused it.

When you’re not there, people usually do one of three things::

  1. They guess the story (and get it wrong).

  2. They waste time hunting for answers.

  3. They ignore the data completely.

You need to leave your voice behind when you’re not there.

Here’s What I Mean by Annotations

An annotation is just text you add directly to your chart to explain what is happening.

It isn’t fancy. It is literally you writing on the chart to make sure people understand what they are seeing. It works like a small road sign. It tells the reader: “Look here. This is important. Here is why.”

Let’s look at how this works in real life.

What Happened vs Why It Happened

Take a look at the image below.

On the left, you see a line chart. It shows the number of studies funded. The line goes up and down, and then shoots way up in 2013.

The chart tells you what happened (numbers went up). But it doesn’t tell you why.

Now look at the right side. Same data. Same chart. But this time, there is a simple note: “2013: New policy introduced.”

Boom. Now you get it. You don’t have to guess. The policy change lines up with the jump. That little bit of text turned a boring graph into a clear story.

The Chart That Almost Caused Panic

Context can stop a misunderstanding. Check out this chart about help desk tickets.

On the left (the “Before” version), you see a gap. The team is receiving way more tickets than they are processing. If a manager sees this, they might panic. They might think the team is lazy or the system is broken.

But look at the “After” version on the right.

There is a direct note: “2 employees quit in May.”

Suddenly, the panic is gone. It isn’t laziness; it’s a staffing issue. The conversation changes from “What is wrong with you?” to “How can we hire people faster?”

Without that note, the data looks bad. With the note, the data makes sense.

When Should You Use Them?

You don’t need to write a novel on every slide. That would be messy. But you should use annotations for the big moments:

  • Spikes and Dips: Did the numbers jump or crash? Explain what happened (e.g., “Server outage” or “Holiday Sale”).

  • Goals: If you are trying to hit a target, draw a line and label it “Goal.”

  • Key Takeaways: If there is one thing you want people to remember, write it right on the chart.

  • Weird patterns: If something strange shows up in the data, explain it.

Let the chart speak for you

We spend hours making our charts look pretty. But if we don’t explain the data, that work is wasted.

Annotations are your safety net. They ensure your data tells the same story on Thursday morning that it told in Tuesday’s meeting.

So, next time you make a chart, don’t just rely on the legend or the title. Write on the chart. Be the narrator even when you aren’t in the room.

title: Stop Using Dual Axis Charts (Unless You Read This First)
subtitle: The truth about one of data viz's most controversial topics
body_html:
If you work with data, you have probably had this debate.

On one side, you have the data purists, like Edward Tufte or Stephen Few. These are the experts who make the rules. They will tell you that putting two different numbers on the same chart (a dual axis chart) is a data crime.

On the other side, you have your Boss. They usually say something like, “I just want to see Revenue and Win Rate on the same slide. Just put them together!”

Dual axis charts are those charts where you have two different scales on the left and right sides, usually with lines that dance across each other in ways that look... let’s say interesting.

So, who is right? And what should you do?

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The Problem with Two Scales

Before we decide if these charts are good or bad, let me show you why people argue about them.

The Crossing Lines Trick

You know when two lines cross each other on a chart? Your brain automatically thinks something important happened there. Like one thing finally beat the other thing.

But that crossing point might mean nothing.

Since each line has its own scale, you can make them cross wherever you want. Change one scale from 0 to 100 instead of 0 to 1000, and boom, the lines cross in a different spot. Or maybe they don’t cross at all anymore.

It’s like magic, but the bad kind that tricks people.

The Size Lie

Here’s another trap. Dual axis charts make it really hard to tell how big things actually are.

Imagine a chart showing how much money the entire world makes (trillions of dollars) next to how much money is in your bank account (maybe a few thousand dollars).

If I put both on a dual axis chart, I can make your bank account look just as impressive as the world’s economy. The lines can grow at the same angle. They look equally important.

But we both know that’s ridiculous, right? Your savings and the world’s GDP are not the same thing at all.

This is why people say these charts are dangerous. You can stretch and squeeze the scales to tell whatever story you want.

So now you can see why people don’t trust these charts.

Okay, So Should You Use Them or Not?

I’ve noticed after seeing tons of these charts that about 95% of them are confusing or misleading.

Not always on purpose. Sometimes people just want to fit everything on one slide. Or they think it looks cooler. Or they genuinely believe the two things are related and want to show that.

But most of the time, two separate charts would have been clearer.

The tricky part is knowing when you’re in that 5% where a dual axis chart actually helps.

When They Actually Work

Okay, so they’re not always bad. Sometimes they actually make sense. Here’s when:

  1. The relationship IS your whole point. Like “when we spent more on ads, our conversion rate went down.” You’re not just showing two trends. You’re showing how they move together. The connection is the story.

  2. The units are totally different anyway. Like temperature and rainfall. One is degrees, one is millimeters. Nobody expects those to share a scale. But here’s the catch: you MUST color code everything. If your temperature line is red, make the left axis labels red too. If rainfall is blue, make the right axis blue. Without these color clues, people get confused fast.

  3. You’re being honest with the scales. You’re not stretching one axis way up and squishing the other way down just to force a visual connection that doesn’t really exist.

  4. Your audience can handle it. They know how to read charts carefully and check the axis labels, not just look at the pretty lines.

  5. It’s a standard format people recognize. Like a Pareto chart with bars showing counts, and a line showing the running percent as you go. People in business know how to read these already.

What Should You Do Instead?

This is where it gets practical. Let me give you better options that work most of the time.

Small Multiples (My Favorite)

Just make two charts and stack them on top of each other. They both use the same time line at the bottom (x-axis).

It works because you can still see if things go up or down together. Your eye naturally compares them. But you’re not messing with scales or tricking anyone.

Scatterplot for Real Relationships

If you really want to show how two things relate to each other, use a scatterplot (a dots chart).

It directly shows the connection. You can actually see if there’s a pattern or not.

Indexed Charts

Turn both numbers into a starting point number. Like “100 equals our starting point.” Now they’re on the same scale and you can compare them fairly.

This still has some issues, but at least you’re being upfront about what you’re doing.

Two Separate Charts

Sometimes the easiest answer is the best one. Two clear charts often beat one confusing chart every single time.

Here's What I Think

Look, I’m not going to tell you to never use dual axis charts. That would be too simple.

But I will say this: if you’re thinking about using one, pause for a second.

Ask yourself: “Am I using this because it genuinely tells the story better? Or am I using it because I want to fit more stuff on one slide?”

Most of the time, the two separate charts will win.

The goal isn’t to make charts that look impressive. The goal is to help people understand your data quickly and correctly.

If a chart makes things more confusing, even if it looks cool, it’s not doing its job.

title: You're Probably Deleting Too Much From Your Charts
subtitle: And it's making them harder to read
body_html:
There is a popular chart rule. It comes from Edward Tufte.

He calls it the “Data-Ink Ratio.”

The name sounds fancy, but the rule is actually very simple. It says you should look at your chart and ask one question: “Is this ink showing data?”

If the answer is no, you should erase it.

This rule says you should remove the borders. You should remove the gridlines. You should remove the background colors.

In theory, this is a great idea. No one likes a messy chart. But there is a problem: It is possible to take it too far.

Why We Needed This Rule

To understand this rule, you have to look at history.

In the 1980s, computers were just starting to make charts. People went wild with designs. Charts had thick black borders, heavy gridlines, and 3D effects that made your eyes hurt. Some charts even had pictures of coins and briefcases floating around.

It was a mess.

Tufte looked at this chaos and said, “Stop. Just show the data.” He was a hero. He saved us from “chart junk” that made things hard to read.

But that was 40 years ago. Today, some people follow his rule like it is a religious law. They strip a chart so bare that it doesn’t look like a report anymore. It looks like abstract art.

You Can Go Too Far

When you delete everything except the data, you create a new problem.

You end up with just a few floating bars or lines in a big, empty white space. Without any lines to guide you, your brain has to work much harder.

  • You have to guess how tall a bar is.

  • You have to guess which labels belong to which dots.

  • You feel lost because there is nothing to anchor your eyes.

If you make it too simple, it actually becomes confusing.

Good Ink vs. Bad Ink

We need to learn the difference between Junk and Scaffolding.

Junk is bad. This includes 3D shadows, dark borders, and silly pictures. You should definitely delete these.

Scaffolding is good. Scaffolding is the structure that holds your data up. It includes:

  • Light grey gridlines: These help you read the exact numbers.

  • Axis lines: These anchor the chart so it doesn’t look like it is floating away.

  • Background colors: A subtle grey box can help group related charts together.

These things are not data. But they help your brain organize the information. They tell your eyes, “Look here, these things go together.”

Clarity is King

We need to change our goal.

Don’t try to use the least amount of ink possible. Instead, try to make it easy to read

Think about the “Signal-to-Noise” ratio. The Signal is the data and the clues that help you understand the numbers. The Noise is anything that distracts you.

A light gridline that helps you read a number is a signal.

An arrow pointing to a key insight is a signal.

If adding a little extra ink, like a border or a background color, helps your boss understand the chart in two seconds instead of ten, then do it.

So, What Should You Do?

The Data-Ink Ratio is a great starting point. It teaches you to ask questions about everything on your chart.

But remember, you don’t get bonus points for having the cleanest chart. You get bonus points for making a chart people can actually understand.

So, go ahead and keep the scaffolding. Help your readers. Make it clear.

That is ink well spent.

title: Visualization is Part of Data Cleaning
subtitle: It's actually one of your best cleaning tools
body_html:
Most people think data cleaning and data visualization are two totally different things.

Usually, you think cleaning happens first. Then, you make your charts later.

What most people miss is that visualization is not just the last step. It’s actually one of your best cleaning tools.

Let me explain.

Your Chart Sees Things You Don't

Here’s what usually happens when we’re cleaning data. We open our Excel file. We check for missing values. We look for duplicates. We scroll through our spreadsheet. Everything looks fine.

Then we make a chart. And suddenly... wait, what’s that weird spike? Why is there a dot way up there by itself? Why does this line go crazy in March?

Your chart just found problems that your eyes completely missed when you were staring at rows of numbers.

This happens all the time. And it’s not because you’re bad at data cleaning. It’s because our brains are amazing at spotting visual patterns but terrible at spotting patterns in lists of numbers.

What Happens When You Draw Your Data

It helps you find the odd one out

Let’s say you have a list of people’s ages. You ask Excel for the average age. It says “35.” That sounds fine. You think the data is clean.

But if you drew a simple picture, like a dot plot, you would see something shocking.

Most of the dots are clustered around age 20, 30, and 40. But way up at the top of the chart, there is one single dot at “200.”

Wait a minute. People don’t live to be 200. That is an error.

Maybe someone typed an extra zero. Maybe it’s a placeholder code. If you only looked at the average, you would never know that this error existed. But when you look at the chart, the error jumps right out at you.

It shows you what is missing

Sometimes, the problem isn’t what is there. It is what is not there.

Imagine you are tracking sales for a coffee shop. You look at your spreadsheet and see a few empty cells. You think, “No big deal, I will just fill them in with zero.”

Stop! Put that data into a chart first.

When you plot the missing data on a timeline, you might see a pattern. You might notice that all the empty spaces happened on the exact same Tuesday.

Now you have a clue. Did the cash register break that day? Was the shop closed for a holiday?

If you just filled the empty spots with zeros without looking, you would ruin your data. The chart tells you the story of why the data is missing.

Missing values don't always spread out evenly. Sometimes they happen only in one region, only after a certain date, or only for one product type. A simple chart that shows missing counts by group can reveal the pattern.

It catches spelling mistakes

Computers are very literal. They think “Apple” and “apple” are two completely different things because one has a capital letter and one does not.

If you have a column for “City Names,” looking at thousands of rows in a spreadsheet is hard. You will get tired and miss things.

Instead, make a simple bar chart that counts how many times each city appears.

Suddenly, you see a big bar for “New York” and a tiny little bar next to it for “New york” (lowercase). You might even see a bar for “NY.”

The chart makes these typos obvious. It groups them together so you can see that you have three different names for the same city. Now, you know exactly what you need to fix.

It helps you understand distributions

Is your data normal? Skewed? All bunched up in one area?

You need to know this stuff before you start analyzing. It changes what methods you can use.

A histogram shows you in 3 seconds what would take forever to figure out from numbers alone.

Why This Will Save You Hours of Work

When you visualize your data while you’re cleaning it, you start to really understand what you’re working with. You’re not just clicking around and hoping it works. You’re actually looking at your data from different angles.

You catch problems earlier. Way earlier. Before they mess up your entire analysis.

You build better instincts. After you’ve done this a few times, you start to know what to look for. You develop a sense for when something looks off.

You save time. I know it seems like making charts during cleaning would slow you down. But trust me, it’s way faster than finishing your analysis, making your final charts, and then realizing your data was dirty the whole time.

My Simple Process Now

Here’s what I do, and it works so much better:

Step 1: Load my data and do the basic checks. Duplicates, obvious blanks, data types.

Step 2: Make some quick visualizations. Histograms for numbers. Bar charts for categories. Line charts for time stuff.

Step 3: Look at those charts and ask “what looks weird?”

Step 4: Go fix the weird stuff.

Step 5: Visualize again. See if it looks better.

Step 6: Repeat until things look right.

It’s like a conversation between you and your data. The visuals help your data “talk” to you.

You Don’t Need Fancy Charts for This

I’m not talking about making beautiful dashboards here.

Your cleaning visualizations can be ugly. They can be basic. Nobody else needs to see them.

A simple scatter plot works. A basic bar chart works. Even just sorting your data and making a line chart works.

The goal isn’t to impress anyone. The goal is to see the data clearly, so you can clean it well.

The One Thing to Take Away

If you’re cleaning data without visualizing it, you’re basically cleaning in the dark.

Sure, you’ll catch some problems. But you’ll miss a lot too.

Your charts are like turning on the lights. Suddenly you can see the dust in the corners, the stains on the floor, all the stuff you need to fix.

Stop treating visualization like it only belongs at the end. It belongs everywhere. Especially in your cleaning process.

Your data will make way more sense. I promise.

title: The Insight Nobody Wants to Hear (But Everyone Needs)
subtitle: Sometimes, the best insight is knowing there's no insight at all
body_html:
The data industry has an obsession. We are obsessed with “actionable insights.”

It feels like we all have to be detectives. Every time we look at a spreadsheet, we think we need to solve a mystery.

Your manager wants an insight. Your client wants an insight. That random “Data Guru” on LinkedIn definitely wants an insight.

We are told that if a chart does not tell you to change something, it is useless.

But sometimes, the data is just telling you that everything is fine.

And that is actually a good thing.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

What if Doctors Worked Like This?

Imagine you go to the doctor for a checkup. The doctor checks your heart and your blood pressure. She looks at her clipboard and smiles.

“Everything looks normal,” she says. “You are healthy.”

Now imagine you get angry. Imagine if you said, “That is not actionable! Give me surgery! Give me pills! Find something wrong with me so I can fix it!”

That sounds crazy, right? If a doctor made up a problem just to make the visit feel worth it, that would be wrong.

Yet, this is exactly what we do with data. We feel bad if we report that “business is healthy.” So, we start inventing problems.

Your Brain Plays Tricks on You

When you force an insight that is not there, your brain starts playing tricks on you. There is a fancy word for this called apophenia.

It sounds complicated, but it is simple. It is like when you lie on the grass and look at the clouds. You might say, “Hey, that cloud looks like a bunny rabbit!”

Is it a bunny? No. It is just a cloud. But your brain wants to see a shape, so it creates one.

We do the exact same thing with our charts.

Sales dip on one Tuesday. Instead of saying “sales are stable,” we squint our eyes. We say, “Oh look! Sales are down on Tuesdays. This is a pattern! We need a new Tuesday strategy!”

Most times, three dots do not make a pattern. You are just seeing bunnies in the clouds.

Signs You’re Trying Too Hard

How do you know if you are being a good analyst or just making things up? Here are a few red flags:

  • You are slicing the data too much. You filter by region, then by age, then by eye color, until you finally find a graph that looks scary.

  • You feel relieved, not interested. If your main emotion is “Thank goodness I found something to show in the meeting,” you are probably forcing it.

  • You are writing a novel to explain a chart. Real insights are usually obvious. If you need ten minutes to explain why a 0.5% change is a disaster, it probably isn’t a disaster.

The Boy Who Cried “Insight”

Fake insights can cause real problems.

If you shout ‘Emergency!’ every time the numbers move a little, you become the boy who cried wolf. You stress everyone out. You waste time in meetings fixing things that aren’t broken.

Eventually, people will stop trusting you. When a real fire happens, nobody will listen because you treated every tiny spark like an explosion.

Sometimes “Everything’s Fine” is Perfect

We need to change how we think about value.

Value is not only finding problems. Value is also about giving people peace of mind.

It takes real confidence to stand up in a meeting, show a flat chart, and say:

“I have reviewed the data. Everything is stable. The strategy is working. We should carry on.”

That doesn’t mean you are lazy. It means you are honest.

So, take a breath. Stop trying to find a ghost in every machine. Sometimes, the most valuable thing you can tell your team is that everything is okay.

title: The Data You're Not Looking At
subtitle: The WWII lesson that will change how you analyze data
body_html:
During World War II, the military had a big problem. They were losing too many planes in battle.

So they brought in a team of math experts to help. One of them was Abraham Wald.

The military wanted to add armor to their planes. But armor is heavy. Too much armor makes the plane slow and burns more fuel.

They needed to be smart. Where should they put the armor to protect the plane the most?

They studied the planes that came back from battle. They marked where the bullet holes were. Most of the holes were on the wings and the tail.

The answer seemed obvious. Put the armor where the bullet holes are.

But Wald said no.

Put the armor where the bullet holes aren’t, like the engine.

Everyone was confused. The engines didn’t have many bullet holes. Why armor them?

Wald explained it in a simple way. You are only looking at the planes that made it back. What about the planes that didn’t?

Planes hit in the wings came home. Planes hit in the tail came home.

But the planes that got hit in the engine? They crashed. They never made it back to base.

The bullet holes you can see show where a plane can get hit and still survive. The missing bullet holes show you where a plane gets hit and dies.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

We Do This Too

We do the same thing with data. We look at the survey responses we got. But we forget about the people who never answered.

We study the customers who bought our product. But we ignore the ones who looked and walked away.

We analyze the employees who stayed at the company. But we don’t ask the ones who left why they quit.

We’re looking at the planes that came back. We’re missing the ones that crashed.

Listen to What's Not There

Let me show you what I mean.

Your team sends out a survey. You get 1,000 responses. You analyze them and find out that 90% of people are happy with your product. Amazing, right?

Wait.

How many people got the survey? 10,000.

That means 9,000 people didn’t even bother to reply.

Those 9,000 silent people might be so frustrated they did not want to reply. They might already be looking for a different product. They might be your real problem.

But if you only look at the 1,000 responses, you’ll never know.

The empty rows are trying to tell you something. You just have to listen.

How To See What Everyone Else Misses

You don’t need fancy tools to fix this. You just need to change how you look at the screen.

Every time you analyze data, ask yourself one simple question: Who or what is NOT in this dataset?

Here are some ways to find the answer.

  1. Compare your data to the whole group. If you have 500 survey responses, check how many people you sent the survey to. The gap between those two numbers is important.

  2. Look at your funnel. Don’t just celebrate the people who converted. Study the people who dropped off at each step. Where did they leave? Why did they leave?

  3. Check for patterns in who’s missing. Are certain types of people not showing up in your data? Maybe younger users aren’t responding. Maybe people from certain regions aren’t buying. That’s a clue.

  4. Ask why people opted out. If someone unsubscribed from your emails or left your platform, find out why. The people who leave often know more than the people who stay.

Beyond The Chart

Anyone can make a chart based on the numbers in front of them. That is the easy part.

But the best analysts are the ones who notice what is missing. They look at the empty rows and realize something is wrong.

Don’t just count the hands that are raised. Ask why the other hands are down.

title: Why I'd Hire an Excel User Over a SQL Expert
subtitle: The one skill that makes you irreplaceable as a data analyst
body_html:
I would rather hire an analyst who understands how our supply chain works and uses Excel, than a SQL genius who does not know what “gross margin” means.

This is the secret that most hiring managers won’t tell you.

Technical skills are important, but lots of people have them now. Almost anyone can learn the basics of SQL in a few weeks. AI tools can even write the queries for you now.

So, the thing that makes you stand out is not how complex your code is. It is how clear your thinking is.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

SQL is just the delivery truck

Think of your technical skills like a mail truck. The truck is useful because it carries things from one place to another. But the truck is not the important part. The package inside is the main thing.

In data, SQL is the truck. It is the tool you use to move information around. The “package” is the business value. It is the answer that helps the company save money or grow.

If you drive a fancy, fast truck but you deliver an empty box, you haven’t helped anyone. But if you walk over and hand deliver a box of gold, everyone is happy.

The wrong answer to the wrong question

The best code in the world is useless if it answers the wrong question.

You can spend three days writing a query that joins twenty tables and runs perfectly. That is impressive technical work. But if you solve a problem that nobody cares about, you have just wasted your time.

This happens when analysts focus on the how, and forget the why.

Your unfair advantage

This is where domain knowledge comes in. It just means understanding how your industry works.

It means knowing what drives sales. It means knowing what costs money. It means knowing what your customers actually care about.

If you work in retail, it means knowing why some products sell better in the summer than in the winter. If you work in healthcare, it means understanding patient wait times. If you work in tech, it means knowing why users cancel their subscriptions.

Most people do not bother learning this stuff. They would rather take another online course than read their company’s annual report.

This is good news for you. It means that if you do learn the business, you are immediately ahead of the pack.

Put the laptop down and listen

If you want to get promoted, pause the coding courses for a bit. You probably know enough SQL to get the job done. You can learn the fancy tricks later when you actually need them.

To really level up, you need to leave your desk.

Go have lunch with someone from the sales team. Ask them what makes their job hard. Sit with a product manager and ask them what the customers are complaining about. Read your company updates, reports, or leadership notes.

When you understand the problems the company is facing, your SQL skills become much more powerful. You stop being just a person who types code. You become a partner who solves problems.

Changing the way people see you

When you make this shift, something amazing happens.

People start coming to you before they even know exactly what data they need. They trust you to figure out the right question. You get invited to strategy meetings, not just to take notes, but to share ideas.

Your queries actually get simpler, not more complex, because you know exactly what matters.

So yes, learn SQL. It is a great skill. But remember that it is only a tool. Your brain and your knowledge of the business are the real value.

title: Half the Story Is Still a Lie
subtitle: Every good decision has a cost. Show it before someone else does
body_html:
Every choice we make is like a deal with the world. When you pick one thing, you are always giving up something else.

If you want to save money for a new bike, you cannot buy candy today. If you want to stay up late to watch a movie, you will be tired tomorrow morning. This is called a trade-off. It is how life works, and everyone knows it.

But at work, we may act like trade offs do not exist. This is a mistake that can ruin your trust with others.

It feels good to sell a dream

When you want to convince your boss or your team to do something, it is tempting to only show the good news. You want them to see the shiny side of the coin.

We see this happen with data all the time. You might show a chart that looks perfect. You show the numbers going up. You skip the messy part where you explain what the data cannot tell you.

Imagine you find a way to save your company $200,000 a year by switching to a cheaper supplier. That sounds amazing. It feels like an easy win. So you present the savings and everyone gets excited.

But you left something out. The cheaper supplier is slower. The materials are not quite as strong.

Six months later, customers start to complain. Returns go up. The savings are gone because of the new problems. Now, your boss looks back at your report and feels tricked. You did not lie, but you did not tell the whole truth.

Your team is smarter than you think

When you hide the downside, you are just waiting for the bad news to hit everyone later. And when it hits, your story collapses.

The people you work with are smart. They know that nothing is perfect. If you tell them a plan has zero flaws, they get suspicious. They start looking for the trap.

But when you show them the trade-off, you treat them like partners. You let them choose their own struggle. Most people are happy to work hard or pay a price if they know why they are doing it.

Admitting a downside does not make you look weak. Actually, it makes you look strong. It shows you have thought things through. It shows you are someone people can trust

A simple way to tell the truth

You do not need to be negative to be honest. You just need to tell the full story. You can use this simple three-step pattern to make your point without scaring people away.

First, say what we gain.

Be clear about the benefit. Explain exactly why this idea is good.

Next, say what it costs.

Name the downside clearly. Don’t hide it in small print. Say, “The new tool is great, but it is hard to learn at first,” or “This saves money, but delivery will take two days longer.”

Finally, say why it is still worth it.

Show that you have weighed the good against the bad. Explain why the gain is bigger than the cost.

Building a story that doesn’t break

In the end, the best way to keep people on your side is to be the person who tells it like it is.

When you own the trade-off from the start, you are safe. No one can come back and say you hid something, because you never did. You build a reputation as someone who can be trusted, and that is worth more than any quick win.

title: Your Dashboard Has A Reading Order
subtitle: Stop putting your most important charts in the wrong place
body_html:
Most people look at a screen the same way they read a book.

They start at the top left, move their eyes to the right, and then drop down a line. They do this over and over until they reach the bottom of the page.

It is just how our brains work.

This means the moment someone opens your dashboard, their eyes are already moving. They will treat whatever is in the top left as the most important thing.

The question is, did you put the right thing there?

The Mistake Almost Everyone Makes

We know how people read, but we forget it when we build dashboards.

We get deep into the data. We clean the data and test out a chart. When that first chart is finally done, we drop it right in the top left corner. Then we make the next chart and put it right next to the first one.

We keep doing this until the page is full. We build the whole dashboard based on the exact order we finished our work.

This habit is completely normal, but it hurts your message.

Now think about the reader. It is like putting your main point on page eight because you wrote it last.

If your best finding is hiding at the very bottom of the screen, people might never see it. They will look at your first random chart, feel confused, and give up before they find the real story.

Treating Your Dashboard Like A Story

You can fix this easily by changing how you lay things out. Every good story has a clear start, a middle, and an end. Your dashboard should work the exact same way.

The top left corner is your best spot. It is the very first place eyes land, so the whole top row should act like a giant headline. This is your beginning.

Put your most important numbers right here to tell people what happened in just five seconds. A simple message like “Sales are down 12% this month” is clear and impossible to miss.

The middle of your screen is where you back up your big headline. This is the perfect home for your main charts, trends, and comparisons. You are simply showing your audience why that top number looks the way it does.

It gives them the background they need to fully understand the story.

Finally, the bottom of the page is the end of your story. This is where the fine print goes. Save your long tables and extra notes for this area. People will gladly scroll down when they want to dig into those smaller details.

When you set up your page this way, everything feels completely natural, and your audience never has to guess where to look.

The Best Way To Help Your Audience

You might think you are just someone who works with data, but you are actually a designer. The way you place your charts changes how easily people understand your hard work.

Your dashboard already has a reading order, even if you did not plan it. What matters is if that order helps your audience or slows them down.

Start at the top left. Put your most important insight there. Build the rest of the story around it. And the next time someone says your dashboard is confusing, you’ll know exactly where to look first.

title: AI Can Write Your SQL, But It Cannot Do Your Job
subtitle: What actually makes a data analyst irreplaceable in the age of AI
body_html:
A lot of data analysts are scared right now. And honestly, that makes sense.

Every week, a new headline says AI can do everything. It can write code, build dashboards, and clean data. The list keeps growing.

When a tool can do all of that, it can feel like there is nothing left for you to do.

Yes, AI can write code. It can run queries, create charts, and summarize numbers faster than any human.

But two things are still hard for AI. It cannot truly understand your business. And it cannot walk into a room and convince people to take action.

Those two things are called domain knowledge and storytelling. Right now, they are the most valuable things you can bring to the table as a data analyst.

Thanks for reading Explain the Data! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

AI Is Genuinely Good at Some Things

Let’s be fair about what AI is good at. Tools like ChatGPT and Gemini are great at technical tasks. They can write a SQL query from a simple prompt. They can fix your Python code. They can even build a chart if you give them the right instructions.

They save a lot of time on boring, repetitive work.

A study from MIT found that people using AI finished work faster and got better results. But doing things fast and writing clean code is only a small part of what makes an analyst valuable.

What AI Cannot Know About Your Company

AI only knows the information you give it. It does not know your company history. It does not know that sales dropped because your biggest client left. It does not know that a giant snowstorm closed your stores last winter.

This is where domain knowledge comes in.

Domain knowledge is the stuff you pick up from being inside the business. It lives in conversations, meetings, and the small details you notice over time. None of it shows up in a database.

“The goal is to turn data into information, and information into insight.”
- Carly Fiorina, Former CEO of HP

That gap between information and insight is exactly where domain knowledge lives. It is not something you type into a prompt. It comes from being inside the business, paying attention, and building up knowledge over time.

The Work That Happens Before You Open Any Tool
